ALLEGED DESIRE OF VENEZUELA TO DEAL DIRECTLY WITH GOVERNMENTS PURCHASING OIL-CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question for the Prime Minister will perhaps have some direct bearing on the possible consequences of the trip he took to South America. Since the government of Venezuela had indicated prior to the Prime Minister's visit to that country that they would prefer direct government to government dealings on oil exports without going through the oil company middle men, could the Prime Minister indicate if in his discussions in Venezuela he indicated Canada's support for this idea?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ALLEGED DESIRE OF VENEZUELA TO DEAL DIRECTLY WITH GOVERNMENTS PURCHASING OIL-CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker the answer is yes but perhaps not in the areas which would be more directly interesting to the hon. member. I indicated that officials of Petro-Canada would be meeting with Venezuelan officials in the immediate future. The vice-president of Petro-Canada was in the group which visited Venezuela, and he has already engaged in discussions with the Venezuelan government. But beyond an assurance exchanged by both governments that we were interested in each other as a secure source and a secure market, there were no precise plans made for Petro-Canada to buy any quantities of petroleum.
The Venezuelans are interested at this time in seeing that Canada keeps up, more or less, its traditional liftings from Venezuela. This result has now been achieved. As to who the buyer should be, the hon. member knows that Petro-Canada, under the legislation, is empowered to embark on such contracts but they do not seem the likely avenue at this time. Petro-Canada does not own any refining capacity in Canada and it would not be of great advantage if Petro-Canada were to buy their bulk petroleum.

the first reading of Bill C-426, to amend the Income Tax Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker this is an act to amend the Income Tax Act and it arises as a result of a decision in the case of PPG Industries Canada Limited v. the Attorney General of Canada.
This bill would repeal an exception to the guarantee in the Income Tax Act that information obtained from private persons for income tax purposes would be confidential except for the purposes of prosecution under the Income Tax Act. In 1966 the Income Tax Act was amended to provide that private information obtained in confidence by the Minister of National Revenue for income tax purposes could be used by the government in any criminal proceedings whatever, and against any persons as well as the person from whom the information was obtained.
In consequence of this 1966 amendment, serious abuses occurred. In other words, information which is confidential and private which is filed by taxpayers could be used for other purposes, and the purpose of this act is to plug this hole so that privacy is not invaded.

The Ministry of Transport is responsible for the provision of short to medium range airlifts of the Governor General, Ministers of the Crown, Members of the Royal family or foreign dignitaries visiting Canada, Parliamentary Committees or Delegations on official business and, from time to time, federal officials on government business. These flight operations are mainly confined to the North American continent. For its part, the Department of National Defence operates an air service for the transportation of its personnel. However, on occasion, it is called upon to provide special flights for other government departments. This occurs when the demand for such airlifts exceeds the Department of Transport's capacity, or when a transoceanic air airlift is required, since MOT's service is primarily limited to domestic operations. As just mentioned, the Department of National Defence operates certain regular flights of armed forces aircraft to Europe. Unassigned space is made available upon application to Members of Parliament at no cost. The aircraft are manned by crews made of public servants or of members of the Canadian Armed Forces or both. It is not deemed to be in the public interest or in the interest of the traditions of a non-political public service to answer questions calling for the names of such persons. Except during general election campaigns, the Prime Minister, when travelling by air, uses government-owned aircraft. This policy is based on the practice of successive former Prime Ministers, who, when travelling about Canada, had the use of a private railway car owned by the Government. In May 1968, the Prime Minister, following the practice adopted by his predecessor, issued guidelines governing the use of official aircraft by Ministers during a general election campaign. These guidelines, which still prevail, provided that official aircraft were not to be used for purposes related to the election campaign. This means not merely that government business must be involved in any such journey but that official aircraft may be used only when the performance of government business is the sole public purpose of the trip. The reasons that the Prime Minister travels in government-owned aircraft, except as provided above, are that he often requires travel facilities on short notice, he should be able to come back at once to Ottawa in cases of a national emergency, he often requires privacy so that he and his staff may work while travelling, he wishes, as a rule, to avoid inconveniencing the travelling public on commercial airlines and he has been advised that government facilities should be used for security purposes (see page 8618 of Hansard for December 11, 1973). Information about the official trips of the Prime Minister both within Canada and abroad is communicated to the media as a matter of course. Details concerning the destination, purpose and general duration are made public. For security reasons, both for the Prime Minister and accompanying persons and for crew members, it is deemed preferable not to disclose too precise details such as actual departure and arrival times, stops en route, itinerary, place of accommo-

It will take me a little while to swallow that. However, we all love the parliamentary secretary and know he is trying to make his points, so we will forgive him.
There has been a curious addition to this debate which is very appropriate to discuss on motions 1 and 12. It is rather unfortunate that I was handed this press release unsigned. It looks as though it came from some government department. However, I think it was in a Reader's Digest envelope. It was handed to me just as I entered the House, although the subject has been current for some time. I wish to put this on the record because it will have some effect on how the debate goes. Then I will have some questions to pose to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) and, hopefully, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen). Perhaps we could resolve quite a number of questions on the matter of content vis-a-vis publications, leaving aside those issues having to do with broadcasting. The news release reads as follows:
It was announced by Reader's Digest today that, after an examination in depth of the interpretation and application of section 19 of the Income Tax Act as it will apply if and when Bill C-58 is adopted, and, after discussions with officials of the federal government, it has come to the conclusion that the steps it has already taken or under way to conform to the amended statute, will permit it to continue to publish its French and English editions in Canada in such a way as to have them classified as Canadian issues of Canadian periodicals for income tax purposes.
The result will be, it stated, that advertisers in its periodicals will continue to have the right to deduct their expenses for advertising space for income tax purposes.
I do not know what ruling has been made, but I am sure parliament is entitled to know. This is rather a key question. I am not even remotely suggesting there is anything underhanded about this. I want to know, and the House is entitled to know, what bargains have been struck by the Minister of National Revenue and his officials to make Reader's Digest feel that it can live with the content rule. I think this is extremely apposite.

I shall not continue at this stage for very long if the minister indicates he will be giving a substantive answer to this question. I am somewhat upset by the fact that in general one can apparently jettison a principle-that is, the 80 per cent content rule-or that those of us who have resisted the content aspect of this legislation should have to cease to make the points we want to make just because Reader's Digest has had some discussions with officials which makes it comfortable with Bill C-58. It does make it rather awkward to carry on the debate, not knowing what the undertakings have been. I think we are entitled to know what the discussions were.
I must say that the officials of the department were very frank and forthcoming-which is in the best traditions of the public service of this country-when they appeared before the committee, but I want to know, and the House is entitled to know, what has happened since to make Reader's Digest able to live with the bill. If the hon. member has something to say, perhaps he will say it in a moment. This is quite a serious point. It will seriously affect the length of this debate if the minister is able to give us an assurance.
We all know Reader's Digest has filled our offices with an alarming amount of paper telling us about the difficulty they would have. Now, after discussion with officials of the federal government, they have come to a different conclusion. We would like to know the purport of the discussions and how Reader's Digest is now able to take such an about-face: it is almost a faster about-face than this government made with regard to wage and price controls from 1974 to 1975.

speechtext:
As I indicated, the press release was issued in October, 1975, and following my appearance before the standing committee there were several questions raised about the uniqueness of digests. We indicated there, and have indicated publicly, that it was not the intention of the legislation as produced by my hon. colleague to preclude the operation of a digest in Canada. As a result of questions which were raised in the committee as to whether this legislation in fact had that effect, I again discussed the matter with my officials and subsequently talked to counsel for Reader's Digest.
It seemed to me at the time that the legislation would have that impact, that is, that it would preclude digests, so that if two, three or ten Canadians got together and decided they were going to have a Canadian digest 100 per cent owned by Canadians, with the editing and publishing being done in Canada, it would be theoretically possible for them to operate in Canada under the 80 per cent rule, but it would be for all practical purposes impossible because of the unique nature of digests.
I then discussed this at some length with counsel for Reader's Digest and I asked them also to discuss it with my officials. At that time it seemed really academic, because Reader's Digest had indicated publicly through Mr. Zimmerman that it did not intend to abide by the 75 per cent ownership rule. That being the case, any discussion about content and the 80 per cent "not substantially the same" rule seemed to be really an exercise in futility because they were not prepared to go down this route. In conversations with counsel for Reader's Digest we more or less operated on the basis of assuming that that in fact will take place.
We have a proposition, or a proposal to make that we can abide by the 80 per cent rule provided it is clearly understood that if the United States Reader's Digest secures its material from American or, for that matter, British magazines and that material is used in the U.S. Reader's Digest, and if that same article was condensed and used in the Canadian one, would that be considered as 80 per cent different? We considered that and decided, because of the unique nature of digests that we would accede to that, so the 80 per cent rule holds.

No, Mr. Speaker, the rule stands. I have had some criticism of the fact that I said the 80 per cent rule is an interpretation. It is an interpretation. It is not an amendment to the regulations, as has sometimes been indicated in the press. It is an interpretation that was given about the meaning of "not substantially the same". Because it was an interpretation, I felt I had to have the backing of my cabinet colleagues on it. I indicated, as a courtesy to publishers and those who might consider advertising in these magazines, that if this were challenged through the usual tribunal and it was not substantiated, then it would be the intention of the government to bring in a new notice of ways and means motion to define that "not substantially the same" means 80 per cent difference. But the advertiser who successfully challenged would be able to write it off in the current year. It would not be retroactive.
The reason for indicating this to the publishers was to save the expense and frustration of going down this route, conceivably winning a case and then finding that the government moved in and applied the hammer. This is not an unpredecented move. It has happened on many occasions that a government has indicated it proposed to go a particular route and what the intention of legislation was, then it has been changed by a decision of the courts or a loophole has been found. In order to give effect to the government's intention, the bill has subsequently been amended but not amended to give a retroactive effect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak to motion No. 1. The events of the past few moments underline the wisdom of this motion, the effect of which would be to postpone the effect of this bill until December 31, 1976-a one-year delay. The confusion now existing about the effect of Bill C-58 has just been multiplying. Last May an interpretation was offered by the office of the Minister of National Revenue to the effect that a content of roughly 50 per cent difference would be acceptable. That was overruled by fiat from the office of the Minister of National Revenue, by a press release under his own name in which the 80 per cent content rule was enunciated. That led to great discussion in the committee following second reading of the bill.
February 3, 1976

The committee tried to bring before the government evidence that the 80 per cent rule was unfair, would be ineffective and practically impossible to police. Members of the committee from both sides were disposed to find an accommodation whereby the committee would be able to report a recommendation that the 80 per cent content be reduced. What is happening now is that the bill is to be allowed to stand with the 80 per cent content, but interpreted by the department in such a way that Reader's Digest will be able to continue to publish in its customary manner.
I suggest to Your Honour and to the minister that this is bringing us back to the very situation that Bill C-58 was intended to obviate, namely, the existence of special status for certain magazines. Time and Reader's Digest had special status, and a great effort was made to find a way in which Canadian publications could be enhanced. The method the government submitted was, as was repeatedly said on second reading in the House and in the committee by witnesses of diverse background, an unfair way.
I suggest to Your Honour that at the very least the bill ought to be referred back to the committee in light of the astonishing developments today. If I were the editor of Time magazine for which this bill has disastrous implications, as well as for Reader's Digest until a few moments ago, I would be asking if there was any chance of negotiating with the minister to find a formula through which the interpretation for Time would be allowed in the same way as for Reader's Digest.
I recall, at the committee hearings, the editor and publisher of Time magazine submitted in rough form a proposal for a new Time Canada. Under the changes proposed for that magazine they considered it should be able to qualify under a reduced interpretation. If we are to go along with what has been suggested this afternoon, namely, that Reader's Digest be allowed to continue and meet the requirements of this bill when it becomes law, then I submit the same opportunity ought to be given to Time magazine. I think the same holds true especially for the auxiliary publications also affected by this bill, for whom a great deal of concern was evidenced in committee but which do not hit the public eye as much. I speak particularly of MD of Canada, a magazine of great import to the medical profession which makes a very special contribution to medical knowledge in this country.
Motion No. 1 underlines the necessity of delaying the implications of this bill for one year once it becomes law. Even before that, however, I believe it would be grossly unfair of the government, in light of the interpretation on behalf of Reader's Digest, not to resubmit this bill to the committee for a thorough examination of how the full aspects of interpretation will be ruled on in the case of all publications that would be severely affected.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, wish to speak in support of this particular amendment. Nothing has given greater cause for that support than the words of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) a few moments ago. Having been on the committee, and having seen this bill progress from tragedy to tragedy and chaos to chaos, I feel we have only added fuel to the fire today. The minister indicated that he looks forward to the time when he can make a more definitive statement about his negotia-
Non-Canadian Publications
tions and consultations with Reader's Digest. This has left us in a quandary.
If I understood the minister correctly, if the Canadian edition of a digest, any digest, reprinted an article that had appeared in a parent, whether it be a United States parent or not, which article was directly commissioned by the parent, then it falls within the 80 per cent test. If, however, the journal printing that article had not been directly commissioned, but it had been a condensation or reprint from any other publication in the world, then it would not fall within the 80 per cent rule. I hope the minister will rise on a point of order to correct me if I misinterpreted what he said.
What if an article appeared in the German edition of Reader's Digest or in any other publication: would it be considered? In other words, are our tax collectors directing their minds only to what is happening to the United States parent edition in order to determine whether an article falls within the 80 per cent rule, or will they consider articles in all editions of the Digest?
Second, will the minister explain, hopefully during the debate on the proposed amendment, whether the provision previously referred to relates only to the United States parent edition, or to other editions controlled by the U.S. parent, or is the matter broader than that? Will the authorities go so far as to determine whether the U.S. parent edition has an indirect association or connection with some other publication? For example, if Reader's Digest were to be involved with an interlocking board of directors, with publication XYZ, say, would our tax collector look at publication XYZ because of their association with the Reader's Digest parent company?
I reaffirm what the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Roche) said. Although the minister has denied vigorously the sorts of allegations the hon. member made, it seems to me that Time, in the matter of their negotiations with the Department of National Revenue, were sold down the river. Without doubt, men of honour stood before the committee and said they were left with the clear impression that the content rule was not to be one involving 80 per cent. Subsequently, under what is known as the Cullen rule, they were zapped with the 80 per cent provision. They were knifed in the back with that 80 per cent provision.
I do not want this legislation to be passed in that atmosphere. I do not think legislation should be enacted in an atmosphere of distrust, particularly legislation involving the Department of National Revenue. Although on occasion we have all argued with the Department of National Revenue, that department for many years has enjoyed a reputation of integrity and can be proud of it.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona referred to MD of Canada. One could include other medical publications in what he said. Certainly, we should direct our attention to those publications. What is the position with regard to such publications? I know that the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) feels that he is in a shooting gallery, that foreign publications are daily taking potshots at him. Since the Minister of National Revenue is more sensitive and sensible about this particular issue than his cabinet

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my concern about what is happening. I am very sympathetic toward efforts to encourage Canadian publications, writers and artists in general, but find it difficult to accept what has been put before parliament and what seems to be happening.
The position taken by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) on what is meant by "substantially different", and to what extent a publication must be different in order for its advertisers to claim a tax credit is, in all fairness, substantially different from the position his predecessor seemed to take as stated in the House. Clearly, there is nothing in the bill to prevent the minister's successor, of whatever political stripe, or his colleagues in government from redefining what "substantially different" means. Surely that is not acceptable to members on either side of this House. That is not how we like to do these things in this country. There is no certainty to this measure. Basically, the government is following an arbitrary procedure.
At the moment I am not expressing any view on the 80 per cent difference rule or content rule. One might accept it in principle; I am not expressing any view on that. One might accept the necessity for some such law requiring Canadian advertisers to use Canadian-owned publications, that is, 75 per cent Canadian-owned, containing material that is 80 per cent different from something printed in the United States, for example. Even if we could agree on that, how many of us can accept the idea that the definition as to what is substantially different can be pulled out of the air by the Minister of National Revenue or his cabinet colleagues and changed from time to time? As it is, there is nothing to prevent their changing it two weeks from now or one year from now. There is nothing to prevent some successor government changing it. That is the point. Surely, this is a most unacceptable way of proceeding.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

I am not attacking the Minister of National Revenue personally. I think he is acting in good faith. The same applies to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner). I accept their sincerity although suggest that they are most misguided on this occasion. This afternoon the Minister of National Revenue gave a good example of how subjective the implementation of this law is to be and will continue to be. In days of old when the law of equity was developing, it used to be said that the interpretation of the law depended on the length of the chancellor's foot. What is meant by "substantially different" will depend on the judgment from week to week, month to month and year to year of the Minister of National Revenue. It will depend on the interpretation of different ministers.
It may be said that we have had in Canada for some time provisions governing broadcasting and Canadian content of broadcasts. At least these provisions are administered in public by a commission which operates in public. It is not-I hope the minister will not take offence-a hole-in-the-corner operation of the kind associated with this legislation. That is how it is to continue. The minister has

indicated a tendency which would make it possible for Reader's Digest to continue to operate. I do not want to dissuade him, because I happen to think that Reader's Digest should continue to operate. Nevertheless, the ruling in question is peculiar.
The test as to whether something is different, as I understand it, depends on its origin, not whether it happens to be the same as something being published in the United States, for example. Are we to have a succession of ingenious developments of this sort in relation to the application of this bill? I say as earnestly as I can, and without wishing to take too much time, that the 80 per cent provision is not embodied in any statute. It is only something which came out of the mind of the minister or the minds of his colleagues. It is arbitrary in that sense. It is also completely arbitrary in the sense that it can be changed whenever the minister changes his mind or whenever his cabinet colleagues change their minds. In that event there is to be no public discussion: there is to be a nice, cosy discussion within the confines of the minister's office or possibly in the cabinet room.
Is that the way we want to aid Canadian culture and Canadian publications? Is that the way we want to operate in this country? It is a secretive hole-in-the-corner kind of operation; it is fundamentally and totally arbitrary. I cannot support it. The government should think longer about this. I believe the motion calls for a deferral. The most charitable thing I can say for the minister and his colleagues is that they must be totally confused and mixed up or they would never have put this kind of proposition before parliament or this kind of interpretation before this House.
In order to prevent their making fools of themselves in perpetuity, I suggest that they defer further consideration. I suggest that they not impose their large majority upon this House, nor put through something, no matter how well motivated the idea may be. The method of interpreting, application and administering, in view of its arbitrariness and secretiveness, is opposed to the whole Canadian tradition of law and the way we want to see governments doing things.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to speak briefly to this first amendment. I remind hon. members that it does not deal with the matter of "not substantially the same". It deals specifically with the proposition that the bill should be delayed for a
February 3, 1976

further year. I am only going to talk about that particular point. I might say, in passing, that I find the charge of secrecy levelled by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to be something of a specious, hollow and regrettable charge. There has not been a piece of legislation in the ten years I have been in the House of Commons that has been subjected to anything like the searching examination the propositions contained in this rather simple bill have been subjected to, and not only in the House but in the country at large. No other piece of legislation has generated more mail on both sides of the question or more letters to the editor, unless possibly the matter concerning the hunting of baby seals.
This issue has been openly examined in the committee. Officials have been available to answer questions from hon. members. Questions have been asked and interpretations have been given. I regret the fact that in his continuing campaign against this bill and what it is attempting to do, the Leader of the Opposition at this stage of the game has introduced specious charges of secrecy and things of that kind.
When one looks at the proposition that this bill should be given another year's delay, it becomes increasingly difficult to take the opposition seriously. I have had a chance to review the history behind this bill, a bill that is obviously concerned with trying to create equity in the imposition of the tax law in terms of periodicals. That, of course, deals with the whole proposition of trying to provide some assistance to periodicals. One need only go back to 1923 when a Conservative member of parliament, Mr. Hocken, obtained the unanimous approval of the House for his motion that measures be adopted to encourage the publication of Canadian periodicals. From there we go to the regime of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett and the fact that he introduced a tariff. One traces it through reference to the study of the periodical industry in the Massey report. In 1956, a 20 per cent tax on advertising was contained in a budget. There was the reneguing of that tax by the subsequent Conservative government.
A royal commission went into, at length, the needs of this industry and the need to do something. It concluded, in 1961, that a nation's domestic advertising expenditure should be devoted to the support of its own media communications and that a Canadian periodical is one published in Canada, owned either by Canadian citizens or by a company incorporated under the laws of Canada or one of its provinces which is controlled and directed by Canadian citizens and is not a licensee or otherwise substantially the same as a periodical owned or controlled outside of Canada. All that was said back in 1961.
What has been the record of this parliament since then? Has the problem disappeared? Have those problems disappeared that one of the greatest civil libertarians of this country, Gratton O'Leary, studied? Of course not. All that persists in this debate is the obstruction and refusal to act on the part of members of this parliament. This is now being led by members of the official opposition. They can charge secrecy. They can charge that 80 per cent is too high. They can live with 50 or 60 per cent. These are games of arithmetic. However, the problem persists. Therefore, I suggest that this House should reject, and reject in a definitive fashion, any notion or suggestion, and in par-

Mr. Speaker, it may come as some surprise to members of the House that when this bill was first introduced I was at least mildly interested in supporting it. First of all, like many hon. members, I wanted to repatriate foreign industry back to Canada and have as much indigenous publishing industry here as possible and belonging to Canadians. However, as I began to examine the fundamental and underlying issues before us in this debate and in this legislation, I could not help reaching the conclusion that I not only had to oppose this bill, but should oppose it vigorously and do all I could to prevent its passage, or certainly, in the context of this amendment, delay it.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) said there has been no legislation before the House which has enjoyed such openness and examination from all parts of Canada. It may be that the bill has undergone that kind of scrutiny. It is a short bill and, seemingly, a simple and innocuous bill; but the fact remains there are other matters related to it which have not been put openly before the Canadian public. I refer specifically to the kind of negotiations which have been going on behind the scenes between members of the Department of National Revenue and other various elements.

speechtext: Not to mention the Liberal caucus.

speechtext:
Not to mention the Liberal caucus. The fact is, the great difficulty about this legislation is that the so-called Cullen rule is not part of it. This clearly shows the sloppy way in which the bill was drafted in the first place. The former minister of national revenue stated that he would be satisfied with a 50 per cent or 60 per cent content rule. Then, as the committee met to discuss the legislation, the head of the Maclean-Hunter board established under questioning that Maclean-Hunter had interceded with the minister several times for no less than 80 per cent; they would like to have had 100 per cent "substantial difference" but they could live with 80 per cent. I quote from page 25:63 of the committee proceedings, where Mr. Hodgkinson is reported as saying:
We made a suggestion to them that if it was less than 80 per cent the Canadian magazine industry would be in grave difficulty of survival.
That, I suggest to the minister, was not under public scrutiny. These were private, almost clandestine negotiations going on between leaders of the industry and officials of the Department of the Secretary of State and the Department of National Revenue. The Secretary of State can say as often as he wishes that the legislation was open before the Canadian people. The fact is that the operative clauses of the legislation and the rulings have not been under public scrutiny. If the Secretary of State wants to be genuine and serious about openness in this legislation, let him work together with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) and make sure that the ruling will be included in the legislation so that the writers in the publications industry may know exactly where they are when they negotiate for magazine articles.

February 3, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
I guess that in times of excitement like this you tend to revert to your previous vocation, and I flip back very easily to the days I was teaching writing and I imagine in my mind's eye hundreds of writers across Canada waiting to know what kind of climate they are entering. It was Aristotle who said a good writer keeps his audience in mind; he always has his audience in mind when he writes. The dilemma which faces the writer in Canada today is; what audience? I think it is an established fact that Reader's Digest and Time have created the largest circulation in Canada, and though some government members would like to have us believe that it is because of the support given by the parent organization in the United States, nothing could be further from the truth.
Mr. Speaker, you can have all the support you like from parent organizations, but if these periodicals were not publishing the kind of material Canadians want to read, there is no kind of support from parent companies which could make them popular magazines. Reader's Digest and Time have been very careful to publish those kinds of articles, that kind of material Canadians want to read, and that is why they have the largest circulation in Canada. It is a tragedy that the one publication in Canada we can leave lying anywhere without having to be afraid of our children reading it is the publication which is under attack. That is the one the Secretary of State wants to make difficult to operate in Canada.
If the Secretary of State really wanted to help writers he would be more disposed to tear down walls than to create them. I have already suggested that the Secretary of State wants to help writers. He said, however, in a statement to his caucus:
Even if Selections were no longer published in Canada, no doubt the French edition presently printed and available in Europe would be available for distribution to Canadian readers.
What kind of a contradiction is that between the public and the private statements of the minister? On one hand he says he wants to help writers and provide a medium in which they can operate in Canada so that they can publish their articles and become known, and on the other he says that if the French edition of Reader's Digest does go out of existence, the French edition can still be sent over to Canada. Is he sucking, or blowing? Is he tickling, or scratching? Does he want to shut down a magazine, or encourage it? He went on to say:
The uncertain short-term consequences of eliminating the tax exemption for advertisers using Reader's Digest must be weighed against the long-term effects for the Canadian periodical industry of eliminating lumpiness in competition and the removal of a major inconsistency in the government's cultural policy.
That makes my hair stand on end. What is the government's cultural policy for us? Is the beginning of its design first to make sure that a few publications can no longer operate successfully in Canada? Does he wish to eliminate that kind of competition and then move on to other areas? The Secretary of State told us in committee that he does have a cultural design for Canada, and he suggested at that time he would make that design available to members of the committee. We have not received it yet, even though it is two months later. Is that his cultural policy for Canada? Frightening! Then he went on to say:
Of all the major consumer magazines in Canada, Reader's Digest is the most cost-effective magazine advertising medium as the table derived

from the Canadian Advertising Rates directory of December, 1974, indicates.
I underline the words "the most cost-effective advertising medium". Do you suppose it has been the most cost-effective advertising medium because advertisers just love Reader's Digest and Time? No. It is because they know that those two periodicals are the two which Canadians most want to buy and read, and they know that in this way their products will get the greatest amount of exposure before the Canadian public.
On the other side of the ledger, we must ask ourselves this question: If Time and Reader's Digest have been so successful, why have other publications not been equally successful? Immediately you cannot help thinking of the dominant periodical in Canada, namely, Maclean's magazine. I would simply suggest that if a publishing company decides to cater to a very urbanite group, in the style that caters to that small select group of urbanite society, especially Toronto urbanites, it must take the consequences of that publication's decision and suffer a small circulation. Apparently Maclean's is not willing to do this.
I suggested in the committee some time ago that the problem in Canada is not a shortage of good writers, and certainly not a shortage of periodicals but, rather, it is the inhibitions which these writers and periodicals face when it comes to circulation. It so happens that Maclean-Hunter denied this vehemently. Of course, they said it was not a circulation problem but rather, other problems including the competition they face. Just by coincidence, next to Time and Reader's Digest, Maclean-Hunter has the largest distributing facility in all of Canada. That is strange.
I suggested in the committee that if Maclean-Hunter is really interested in helping the publication industry in Canada, what it could do is carry piggyback some of the small publications which are finding it hard to get exposure before the Canadian people. I suggested that maybe what they should do if they' want to help these publications is carry them along in the distribution of their own magazine. This would give phenomenal coverage to the small publications. But they said that was not the solution.
On January 7, a month after the committee had met, there appeared in one of the Toronto newspapers an article regarding the magazine distribution industry. It suggested this was virtually a closed shop. We find in this article a statement like this:
A Maclean-Hunter national magazine distributor said he will not provide magazines to a wholesaler operating in the territory staked out by the Maclean-Hunter regional wholesaling subsidiary, Metro News.
Metro News does have a corner on the market. The article continues:
Many have quit dealing with Metro because of dissatisfaction with accounting systems and service. A normal turnover, Metro counters.
Another Maclean-Hunter operation, Maclean-Hunter Distributing, one of the few national magazine and paperback distributing companies not foreign controlled, refuses to provide even Maclean-Hunter's own circulation-hungry magazines to wholesalers trying to crack Metro News' large territory.
There you have an industry that wants a closed shop and a corner on the market, without competition. That is the background to the kind of legislation that we are faced
February 3, 1976

with today. The Secretary of State just last week published a letter, I suppose you could call it but it is more like an article, in the Vancouver Sun in response to a letter written previously by another gentleman. In that article he stated:
I think the point to keep in mind, however, is that a Canadian writer's chances of success in a foreign market are enhanced if first he or she has managed to get established at home and to develop a solid readership in his own market. It is with that objective in view that government support of writers and publishers is being provided.
I would like to ask the Secretary of State how he can prepare that kind of statement when indigenous writers are complaining all the time about competition from American publishers in Canada without the benefit of relief? The minister has not seen fit to look after that dilemma. There are gaps like this in every aspect of the legislation before us. I could go on, but suffice it to say simply that the amendment before us has a lot of wisdom, especially in light of the statement Reader's Digest has issued today, as well as the statement of the Minister of National Revenue. That statement has muddied the waters more than cleared them and we need time to look at the legislation as well as the ruling.
As the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) has already suggested, the bill ought to be sent back to the committee to be re-examined and to find ways to include the ruling, if there is to be a ruling, in the legislation so that the writer in Canada can move out of this world of insecurity to a place where he knows where he is at and does not have to worry about these rulings of the Minister of National Revenue. I distinctly remember members of the committee asking some very specific questions of officials of the Department of National Revenue, who on the spur of the moment made some judgments as to how the ruling would operate in this case. As they gave their answers, the Secretary of State sat there shaking his head, saying "No, no; that is not it". He then proceeded to reinterpret what that ruling would imply for that particular situation.
We go back to the statement that the writer must always have his audience in mind. I would ask, again, what audience is this? Is it the audience that the writer wants to reach in terms of a reading audience? If that is the case, then he is going to enjoy the freedom of expression that all writers in Canada must have if they are to write creatively and artistically and if they are going to write in a way that Canadian people will want to read. If in the meantime, however, they have to interject before their reading public three other voices of the reading audience for which they must account, namely, the Secretary of State's Department, the Department of Justice, and the Department of National Revenue, then I would ask very carefully again, which audience is it for which the writer must account?
The Secretary of State and the Minister of National Revenue can state as often as they want that this is not curtailing writing and that this is not censorhip. Perhaps in a legal sense it may not be, but in a psychological sense regarding the work that goes into the writing and preparing of a manuscript, this is censorship of the most subtle nature. No writer of any artistic or intellectual integrity, or with a creative desire, will want to submit a writing to any publication if first of all in his mind's eye he has to picture before him the scrutiny of a dollar-oriented Treasury
Non-Canadian Publications
Department official or a legally-oriented Justice Department official. That is no way to stimulate the writing profession in Canada and it is no way to stimulate the publishing industry in Canada.
What we need in this country is freedom of expression without bounds and without the deterrent effect of these various levels of government interfering with our writers.
I return to the injunction that this piece of legislation must be sent back to the committee where it can undergo that kind of scrutiny it deserves, or that kind of scrutiny the Minister of National Revenue has given us reason to believe it deserves as the result of his change in ruling today.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) in his intervention this afternoon raised some very interesting points which I think have some important implications for this legislation. While addressing myself to motion No. 1, which would delay the implementation of this bill for another year, I should like to put on record some of my concerns about the statement of the Minister of National Revenue, to which perhaps he will reply when we come to motion No. 2.
I think all members of this House and the people of Canada must realize and keep firmly in mind that Bill C-58 is a piece of legislation, not to decide who will be allowed to publish in Canada but, rather, who will be assisted to publish. An anomaly in our income tax regulations that has existed since 1965 allowed two major publications, Time and Reader's Digest, to qualify for income tax purposes as Canadian magazines when in fact they were not. The legislation seeks to rectify that anomaly.
The purpose and the hope of the legislation is that the advertising revenue that had in the past gone to these two foreign periodicals, or some of that advertising revenue, will be redirected back to Canadian periodicals unless Time and Reader's Digest conform to the principles of what it is to be, a Canadian periodical. When the minister was before the committee he outlined four criteria for qualifying as a Canadian periodical. They were: place of production, ownership, licensing, and similarity to a foreign publication.
To this date neither Time nor Reader's Digest qualify in those terms as being Canadian, although we learned this afternoon just as the debate began that the Minister of National Revenue had worked out a deal with Reader's Digest concerning the fourth criteria, similarity to a foreign publication. As I understood the minister, he said an understanding had been reached by his department and Reader's Digest that if Reader's Digest bought an article from an American or any foreign magazine and did the editing or did the digesting of that article here in Canada, and at the same time if the parent magazine, Reader's Digest U.S., bought an article from the same source and did the editing and digesting in the United States, then the Canadian article would not be subject to the provision regarding similarity to a foreign publication. Although the two magazines may be using and publishing the same article in their magazines, because the editorializing and

February 3, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
the actual digesting was done by Reader's Digest Canada, it then would come under the 80 per cent rule.
If that is so, then it raises another very important question which I should like the minister to clarify. If they worked out that kind of deal with National Revenue, they must at the same time have worked out a revision of the third criteria the minister mentioned to the committee, which is licensing, because under the existing situation with Reader's Digest Canada and Reader's Digest U.S., its parent, the licensing agreement works as follows: Reader's Digest U.S., the parent, has a pool of articles that it digests, and Reader's Digest Canada can draw on that pool of articles.
As part of the licensing agreement between Reader's Digest Canada and the United States, the following provisions must be met: Reader's Digest Canada must first promise to make no changes to editorial material obtained from the U.S. parent company without written consent. Second, the Canadian subsidiary must not distribute material which the parent disapproves of, or use material from any source other than those sources approved by the U.S. parent company.
Third, it must encourage Canadian writers to contribute material which would be of significant interest to international audiences, and submit any such material to the U.S. parent company for publishing consideration. Unless that licensing arrangement has been changed, in no way, even if they make the arrangement now with the 80 per cent "substantially the same" provision, by any stretch of the imagination can we consider Reader's Digest Canada an independent Canadian periodical if it is subject to the three licensing conditions I have just outlined. So I believe it is important that the minister make a statement to this House concerning what changes his department has agreed to with Reader's Digest Canada, not just on the point of similarity to a foreign publication but on licensing, ownership and place of production.
If this deal has been worked out and there have been some changes in the licensing arrangement, and Reader's Digest qualifies under all the other provisions, then we may accept that it is truly by definition a Canadian magazine and that advertisers in Reader's Digest, Canadian edition, will have the tax deduction benefits. However, I think this is still a blow, in one sense, to the Canadian periodical industry because, as was pointed out effectively in testimony before the committee, Reader's Digest and Time magazine for ten years were allowed to have the benefits through the tax system in respect of advertising revenue, and therefore have been able to capture about 50 per cent of the advertising revenue in this country.
We cannot quarrel with this if they comply with the four criteria, but this certainly does not do anything about redirecting some of that huge amount of advertising revenue back to the Canadian magazines which have been struggling for so long against these huge odds and advantages Reader's Digest and Time magazine were able to enjoy over a ten-year period. The point should be raised that what made Time and Reader's Digest so successful, and what gave them such an unfair competitive advantage, was that they were able to get much of their content at reduced rates from their parent company-at a fraction of the cost
[Mr. Symes. j
any Canadian magazine would have to pay if it tried to acquire the same material.
While these two magazines, Time and Reader's Digest, were able to get that kind of advantage of a cut-rate cost for the material, they also had the advantage, as foreign magazines, of being able to qualify under the provisions of the Income Tax Act for deductibility of advertising expenses. This attracted many advertisers to advertise in Time and Reader's Digest, which would not have been the case had these magazines been classified as foreign, because they would not have had that income tax deductibility benefit. So it seems to me that the Minister of National Revenue has much explaining to do about the kind of deal worked out with Reader's Digest as it relates to the four criteria for a magazine qualified as a Canadian edition.
I cannot support motion No. 1, in the name of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), to delay this bill for one year. As was pointed out in committee and on second reading, we have allowed this anomaly in our definition of a Canadian periodical to go on for far too long, so that Time and Reader's Digest have been able to capture most of the advertising revenue of magazines in this country and Canadian magazines are really at the breaking point. They need to attract more revenue, and unless we move to implement Bill C-58 this will not take place. It can only mean the continuing backsliding of the Canadian periodical industry as it hopes to improve and compete with these two giants.
We need a healthy Canadian periodical industry. From the testimony we have heard, if even a fraction of the advertising revenue which now goes to Time and Reader's Digest were diverted by the passage of this bill to the Canadian periodical industry, it could mean the difference between the collapse or the survival of a number of magazines. This is something to be borne in mind. For a country to have a sense of identity and to be able to speak to people both on the west and on the east coast, we need a healthy magazine industry which can interpret Canada to Canadians, not through the eyes of subsidiaries of some foreign magazines.
So I say that there is no time for delay. This issue has been before the House previously. We have had a royal commission studying it and a special Senate committee studying it. Their recommendations were that we move in the direction in which Bill C-58 is moving and that the longer we delay, the worse the situation will become for Canadian periodicals. I think it is important that we pass this legislation. If Reader's Digest and Time want to conform to the legislation and become Canadian magazines, then that is fine; they will be on the same footing as our industry in Canada. But I cannot see the logic of perpetuating an anomaly that allows these two magazines, of all foreign magazines in Canada, to receive benefits under the Income Tax Act which allows their advertisers to receive these benefits while the same benefits are not given to other foreign publications.
We seem to have a lot of concern for these two magazines at this stage. I find it surprising that the same concern and logic was not voiced for other foreign publica-

tions back in 1965 when they fell under the provisions of the Income Tax Act which classified them as foreign magazines, but Time and Reader's Digest did not. It seems important that we move to the speedy passage of this bill. As I said earlier, I certainly want to hear clarification from the Minister of National Revenue as to the deal that has been worked out with Reader's Digest and what has happened not only to the "substantially different" clause but to the licensing provisions which the minister outlined when he was before the committee. I hope that we can dispose of motion No. 1 soon, and that we can have an answer from the minister on those important questions.

Mr. Speaker, in rising on motion No. 1, asking that the bill be delayed for one year, or until December 31, 1976, I would like to make a few comments regarding the intervention of the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner). It was a typical performance by a minister who is again in trouble. He has staggered from crisis to crisis on Bill C-58. He has been trying to ram something through the House for which he has not had the support of his cabinet, his caucus, or his voters, and now he is trying to weasel once again. Then he gets up with a sanctimonious type of approach and goes after the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), suggesting that by asking simple questions the Leader of the Opposition is trying to delay the bill. I really question whether the minister has any right to consider anyone else to be less pure than he thinks he is on this issue.
Before we even started in the committee we were told that closure would be in effect. They did not exactly use closure, but they told us that the bill would have to be out of the committee by Friday. They said that was it; that was all the time we would have. They said, "We will have the bill back in the House prior to Christmas, and it will be rammed through the House because it is to become effective on January 1, 1976." Now we have a retroactive bill on our hands. I say to you very bluntly, Mr. Speaker, that that minister does not have the support of the House. I suggest that if he checked with members of his caucus he would find that he does not have the support of many of them, either. All that happened today clouded the issue further. Whenever we asked questions of the minister in the committee, he became defensive and said that we had to get this bill through the House because the effective date was January 1, 1976.
The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) also supported this bill in committee. I imagine he thought it was the greatest thing since rye bread, and he thought it would be great for the periodical association. Today he asked the Minister of National Revenue for clarification and said that he does not really know what we are debating. Then he turned around and said that his party is in favour of the bill. How does he know what he is in favour of? Throughout our debate on Bill C-58, the argument has been that if the large amount of advertising revenue which Reader's Digest and Time get were given to Canadian periodicals, it would help the Canadian Periodical Association and Canadian writers. That has been one of the basic arguments of the proponents of this bill. Yet if Reader's Digest can continue to advertise and to exist, where does that argument go?

There is less clarity.

I ask the minister, again, whether our interpretation of the deal he apparently has worked out with Reader's Digest is correct. Our interpretation is that if Reader's Digest international commissions an article, that article appears in any Reader's Digest magazine other than the Canadian one and then it subsequently appears in the Canadian edition, it falls under the 80 per cent rule but if, on the other hand, an article appears, for example, in Redbook, is edited and appears in the U.S. edition of Reader's Digest and then subsequently appears in the Canadian edition, is that acceptable?

speechtext: No, it is the other way round.

The minister shakes his head. Obviously my interpretation of his arbitrary rule is wrong. I think it is important that the minister again rise in his place and not only refer to the interpretation but put it into the statute. It is important that this be in the legislation so that we can take a position on it and pass the legislation. With regard to this arbitrariness, what happens when we have a new minister? Will an order in council change it again? Can it be thrown out? I imagine it can be. Any subsequent minister can come along and say that the content rule will not apply at all in order for a magazine to qualify as a Canadian magazine. I submit that that is not the way to go forward with this kind of legislation.
A number of us received by hand-I received mine at 1.50 this afternoon-a press release from Reader's Digest Canada which indicates that a backroom deal has been made which will allow Reader's Digest to continue more or less in the manner it has up to the present time. I quote

February 3, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
from that press release, or that official communique, as follows:
It was announced by Reader's Digest today that, after an examination in depth of the interpretation and application of section 19 of the Income Tax Act as it will apply if and when Bill C-58 is adopted, and, after discussions with officials of the federal government, it has come to the conclusion that the steps already taken or under way to conform to the amended statute, will permit it to continue to publish its French and English editions in Canada in such a way as to have them classified as Canadian issues of Canadian periodicals for income tax purposes.
The result will be, it stated, that advertisers in its periodicals will continue to have the right to deduct their expenses for advertising space for income tax purposes.
There are a number of questions which arise from that statement. What were the discussions with the officials of the Department of National Revenue? What steps were taken other than those Reader's Digest told the members of the committee about-for example, 30 per cent plus now having Canadian ownership? What other steps has Reader's Digest committed itself to, with the minister and officials of his department, in order that it will conform to the regulations which will classify it as a Canadian edition? Also, I believe the minister should state very clearly what long-term agreement, written or otherwise, Reader's Digest has made with National Revenue officials regarding its Canadianization. Is it a ten-year deal, is it in perpetuity, or what?
We should also have a commitment from the minister as to whether the so-called regulations will be put into the statute. We have many questions at the present time, but the major argument, obviously, must be with regard to the arbitrary approach being used. The Secretary of State and the minister are telling us to leave this matter in their hands, to let them make the rules, to let them make the backroom deals, and that we as members of the opposition, and the Canadian people in general, should be satisfied because those two ministers will make the best deal possible. That is what they are saying, and that is not good enough. The matter of the arbitrary manner in which this rule will be interpreted must be discussed and the minister must stand in his place and clearly explain that situation.
For example, when Time was before the committee, it indicated to us very clearly that it had submitted to National Revenue a so-called 50 per cent Canadian and 50 per cent other than Canadian mock-up for adjudication by officials of the department. During the course of the debate on this bill, Time had been under the impression that a 50 per cent content rule, if it could abide by it, would qualify it as a Canadian magazine if the other matters were adherred to. Obviously, the question for the minister is this: Is a backroom deal also being worked out with Time Canada, and in the not too distant future will we have a press release from them indicating that they, also, have been able to flex their muscles and move the minister to get a deal which will also classify them as Canadian? If that is the case, what has been the point of this whole exercise which is taking the time of the House?
Further, what about the licensing arrangement? Has a change been made in the so-called deal for Reader's Digest and Time with regard to licensing? The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie also mentioned licensing. With all this in mind, and considering the long discussions which have taken place, the bill should be referred back to committee for full disclosure and discussion, without the time restric-

tions which were placed upon the committee and without the restrictions which were also placed on government members who wanted to sit on that committee and who were in opposition to the bill.
We saw a charade in committee, the like of which I have not seen in my time here. Long-standing, full-time members of the committee were suddenly bumped because they were going to ask embarrassing questions of the minister and his officials and because they were not in favour of this bill. It is incumbent upon us to lift this bill for one year so that during that period of time full disclosure can be made and the Minister of National Revenue can give us a commitment that the administrative regulations will be incorporated in proposed legislation which can be debated in this House.
I should like to serve notice that I will move that the bill be referred back to committee once we get to third reading stage.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I have not yet taken part in the debate on Bill C-58 it is not because I believe that this legislation is not important; on the contrary this issue is, in my opinion, most important. However I wanted to listen to what my colleagues had to say about this legislation which directly concerns two magazines now published in Canada, namely Time and Reader's Digest. After listening to the interventions for and against this legislation, I can only urge that consideration of the bill be postponed, according to the amendment.
I hope that government members will pay attention to the arguments that were or will be put forward by the members of the opposition for I sincerely believe that no member should support such a legislation which will destroy the freedom of the press in Canada. This bill was introduced by the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) with the view of putting those two magazines on the same footing as other Canadian publications.
Since the publication of the Davey report on mass media, I believe everybody agreed that only truly Canadian publications should be granted tax deduction for advertisements appearing in their columns. So far, Mr. Speaker, I think everyone agrees, and even Time magazine has clearly indicated its intention of being bought off by Canadian interests so as to comply with the requirements of the bill. Selection may have done the same thing, namely become a genuinely Canadian magazine, in spite of its initial lack of enthusiasm for this prospect.
Unfortunately the government allowed itsef to be carried away by nationalist feelings. Not content with trying to make Canadian publications out of Time and Selection by encouraging Canadian interests to purchase them, the government decided to go further and to interfere with the content and the nature of the articles published in those magazines. This in my view, Mr. Speaker, is a gross and unforgivable abuse of power.
We are not in Germany under Hitler's domination nor are we is the USSR under Stalin's, we are still living in Canada, a country where democracy and the freedom of the press should always be very well protected.
Does the present government wish to be remembered as the government that restrained and destroyed the freedom of the press in Canada? It is remembered as a government that has told the newspapers: "Publish 80 per cent of this and 20 per cent of that, but publish this article and not that one because it is not Canadian". And yet that is more or less what is advocated under the stupid Cullen rule which requires that the content of a magazine be 80 per cent
Non-Canadian Publications
Canadian in order that those who advertise in it may obtain income tax deductions. I just cannot find words to say how shocked I am by this unjustifiable intervention of the government in this field where freedom is sacred.
Today, the government requests us to let it control the percentage of Canadian articles in magazines; so what will prevent it from coming back soon and ask us to let it control the ideas expressed in those magazines under the pretext that they are not as consistent as they should be with Canadian ideas?
The step that the government wants to take today with the adoption of Bill C-58 is extremely dangerous. It is a step towards dictatorship. The government should be aware of the dangers that Bill C-58 will create for the future of the freedom of the press and the freedom of speech.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, the government should differ passage of Bill C-58 for a year, as requested in the amendment under consideration today, or the bill should be replaced by some provisions granting tax deductions for advertising space in Canadian-owned publications only. Such a measure would help to reassure all Canadians who rightly wish to see Canadian publications become more prosperous and better able to meet fair competition from foreign publications.
It is very hard for Canadians to understand this government's attitude when it comes to protecting Canadian interests against our powerful southern neighbours. Indeed, the government has no qualms, as far as publications are concerned, in using brutal force to the extent of endangering freedom of the press, while, in other fields where Canadian interests are strongly threatened, it does not even lift a finger.
For example, it is well known that Canadian car rental companies are now facing unfair competition from giant American companies. The Canadian government, far from helping them in that connection, leane them to struggle without any assistance against the giant financial interests of American companies.
The Canadian government is not consistent with itself, not does it appear logical to Canadians. On the one hand, under the pretext of promoting Canadian publications, it puts the blame on the freedom of the press and, on the other hand, it allows Canadian car rental companies to be crushed by American companies. How can we have confidence in the good will of such a government? Further, the minister in charge of the Secretary of State does not deserve any congratulations for the manner in which he has piloted this bill. He repeatedly said in this House in May last that the exact meaning of the words "which is not substantially of the same kind" would be known in advance by the magazines involved. We now know that it was only very late in October-hardly two months before the date it came into force-that the Minister of Revenue made known his interpretation. We also know that, because of the effects, this interpretation-which calls for a Canadian content of 80 per cent-is the most explosive and the most dangerous legislative proposal of all measures now under consideration in this House. Had the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) proceeded with a minimum of competence, he would have taken the trouble to consult the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen)

February 3, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
before presenting his bill. His clumsiness and negligence in this affair are inexcusable. All Canadians know he was talking through his hat last May when he said that the Department of National Revenue was ready to produce its interpretation. And today, Mr. Speaker, all Canadians know that the former Minister of National Revenue was talking about a 50 per cent Canadian content before the present minister introduced the 80 per cent rule. I therefore cannot accept the attitude of the minister responsible for this bill and his performance will no doubt be cited as an example when it comes to showing how to present a bill.
The Secretary of State has been stubborn in his incompetence, and has persisted in the repeated mistakes he has made during the discussion of this bill. I understand the irrritation of the directors of Time and Reader's Digest, when they said:
In the face of uncertainty, we may have to close down ...
-even if today the minister tells us that the publication of the same magazines may go on under some arrangements with the government, but they said they were ready to close down not because they do not want to comply with the law but because they were able to determine with a reasonable minimum of certainty what this bill says.
I would like to come back to the question of the dangers this bill will represent for the future of the freedom of the press in Canada, because this consideration is the most important of all. It is necessary, Mr. Speaker, to insist on the fact that all newspapers in the country are unanimous in condemning firmly the measure put forward by the Government.
La Presse of Montreal says without hesitation: "The measure is "a masterpiece of stupidity". "The Toronto Globe and Mail writes: "A foolish and dangerous censorship". The Edmonton Journal headlines: "An unjustified measure in a free society". And I could quote hundreds of articles and thousands of statements which agree that Bill C-58 is a menace to the freedom of the press and the freedom of speech in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the minister proved himself to be very determined in insisting that his bill be passed, despite the lifting of shields by all who believe in the freedom of the press. Determination is often a quality. But, in this instance, Mr. Speaker, I doubt that it is. It reveals a tragic lack of common sense and realism.
Mr. Speaker, let us reflect for a few moments on the consequences of Bill C-58 if it is applied in its present form. Contents should be 80 per cent Canadian. Let us suppose that in the course of a week, five events occur, namely, war breaks out in the Middle East, Brezhnev resigns or is replaced, a flying saucer really lands in Japan, the Queen of England resigns, and the Prime Minister of Canada decides to build himself an even larger pool. As no Canadian publication can afford to send journalists everywhere throughout the world, and bearing in mind the fact that our newpapers and magazines must respect the 80 per cent Canadian content rule, we stand a chance of getting a paper or magazine 80 per cent of which would be devoted to the Prime Minister's new pool, the four other events being relegated to the last pages.
Mr. Speaker, one sees immediately that the 80 per cent content rule threatens the Canadian people, primarily with

not being properly informed of international events. Who, Mr. Speaker, would ever want that kind of situation? Yet, that will be the result of Bill C-58 if it is applied strictly.
It is as easy to imagine a crowd of officials with a lot of rules trying to read the articles to ascertain that 80 per cent of the pages are filled with Canadian texts. It is really a nightmare, Mr. Speaker. Adoption of this legislation must be delayed or the bill withdrawn by the government. If the government and the Secretary of State persist in their attitudes, I hope there will be enough members in this House to delay the adoption of this bill, which is ridiculous and dangerous.
As a conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I urge the minister responsible to think it over. Is he prepared to leave his name tied to a piece of legislation which directly undermines the freedom of the press and of speech in Canada? Does he want our country to recall him as the man who struck the first blow against the liberties which we hold as heritage since the existence of Canada? If he wants us to remember him by a saying that he was able to preserve those liberties, he must withdraw this bill or delay its adoption as required in the amendment.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members opposite do not realize the difficulties they are apt to encounter from trying to proceed with this legislation at this point in time. There is no reason for this House to be asked to deal with legislation of this kind, especially in view of the information that came to the attention of members of parliament this afternoon as a result of the circular all members received from Reader's Digest. What is to happen to other publications? Other magazines and periodicals will be affected by this legislation. What will happen to TV Guide, to our medical journals and other journals which the Canadian people like to read? You know, I always like to have a new coat before I throw my old one away. I suggest that the House would be well advised to delay this legislation for 12 months, which is what the amendment suggests, and reconsider the entire gamut of the matter.
I have had great respect for the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) and hope what I have to say will not force him to stay out of the House for too long. His statement regarding the 80 per cent content, 80 per cent the same as, or the 80 per cent difference rule-whichever way you want to interpret it-was most unfortunate and dangerous. I don't care what the minister says and I care less for the government. I say emphatically that the minute any government begins to decide what the Canadian people shall read, it becomes very, very dangerous. I am surprised that the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie goes along with the government in this regard. You do not build up the weak by tearing down the strong. It seems to me that there are other ways to help Canadian periodicals develop, other ways to help them become strong.
I am happy to see the Postmaster General (Mr. Mack-asey) in the House. I am sure he knows that increased postage costs have created financial difficulties for many periodicals. The magazine Country Guide is not nearly as large a publication as it once was, mainly because of the cost of postage. I suggest we can support Canadian periodicals in many ways. Why are we not looking at those ways and means of supporting the industry within Canada? I am sure we in the opposition are just as great Canadian supporters as anyone else in Canada. Nevertheless, why do we have to try to tear down the strong in order to build up the weak?
In committee I took issue with a promoter of Maclean's magazine because there was such a large amount of advertising in that periodical. At one point it was 60 per cent, which means 60 pages out of 100. Unfortunately, many of those 60 pages were advertising American liquor. Is the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) saying that it is all right for Canadian magazines to advertise American liquor rather than publicize commentaries that are acceptable, required and in some cases almost necessary because
Non-Canadian Publications
Canadians like them? Many Canadians like to peruse these magazines.
This government would be well advised to really consider this amendment. The bill should be taken out of the House for 12 months and sent back to committee. The minister shakes his head. It is unfortunate that he has become dogmatic and is going to force this issue even though there have been so many inconsistencies. Since the presentation of this bill, changes have been made. We had 50 per cent, 60 per cent, 70 per cent and 80 per cent. This is frustrating for everyone. Why should we have had to wait 12 months on this legislation and then, at the very last moment, a statement has been made? We have no guarantee that the statement will be correct that there is provision for Reader's Digest to survive.
We then came to the point where there is a real problem. Who is to decide that it will be 80 per cent different? I cannot accept this. I believe it is a right of the Canadian people to decide for themselves what they want to read and when they want to read it. If we are going to continue entering into state control in all facets of our way of living,
I suppose we are going to have to accept it. However, just because we are entering into a program of economic control that is to last for three years, we should not have to accept a publishing control that may be for all time.
It is most unfortunate that any minister, not necessarily this Minister of National Revenue, or any government by any whim of fancy can change the whole aspect of this. This is a very dangerous precedent that we are setting here today. I hope the minister and the government will reconsider and accept this amendment. They should take the legislation back to committee where it can be reconsidered once again and adequately amended. This is an unprecedented move. It is beneath the dignity of this House of Commons. I hope the minister will give it further consideration.
