Mr. Speaker, like many of my colleagues, I appreciate the opportuniy of speaking to and supporting this amendment. I spoke at some length when the bill originally came into the House. I pointed out then that I felt the great majority of Canadians thought the bill was very unfair. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who stated that we all agree that Canadian magazines and Canadian writers must-be helped. However, this should not be done at the expense of doing away with Time and Reader's Digest. That is the view of a great many people of Canada, especially the older families.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) mentioned that this bill has generated a lot of mail pro and con. I agree with him to some extent. However, the great majority of mail that came into my office was in favour of continuing Reader's Digest. I would say it was about 25 to 1. I know that at one time I had received about 250 letters. I would point out to the Secretary of State, who is standing in the confessional at the back, that the letters are again starting to come in. Therefore, people must be concerned about this matter.
Many people have questioned the 80 per cent that was set by the government or the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen). They feel that Reader's Digest will not be as

February 3, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
good a magazine. Many people stated in their letters that of all the magazines that came into their houses, Reader's Digest was the only one they really liked and respected. They do not want anything done to change that. I hope the minister gives that matter serious consideration. The directive that was issued today by the Reader's Digest officials came as a shock and a surprise to many members including, I am sure, some on the government side.
Our spokesman for this particular bill, the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) had to leave early in order to visit the constituency of the Secretary of State. I hope he will put the situation to them plainly. The Reader's Digest press release came as a great surprise to many of us. As the House leader of the NDP said, Bill C-58 is thrown in here again. The government does not know from one day to the next what bill it will bring into the House. A great many of us would have been interested in more clarification from Reader's Digest and the Minister of National Revenue on this press release. It might have had some bearing on this debate and might possibly have shortened it.
Many of us are skeptical and worried. As was pointed out by previous speakers, the Minister of National Revenue may interpret the bill one way, but his successors, after reading an article which may be critical of their department of the government, could have another interpretation. In that event, the headsman's axe or the witch hunt would start again.
In today's mail I received a clipping from someone in Regina. I do not know why it was sent to me, when we have so many western members. It came from Grace Stewart, of Regina, who wrote:
Can you possibly help do something about this and help prevent the government pursuing its present collision course with Reader's Digest?
Application of Bill C-58 to Reader's Digest and Time magazine, to deprive the publications of Canadian status, sets a precedent that is frightening.
The legislation to amend section 19 of the Income Tax Act revises the regulations which grant Canadian status to foreign-based newspapers and periodicals.
Not many people will question the authority of parliament to enact the legislation. Application of it retroactively, however, to established Canadian corporations is another matter.
Reader's Digest and Time magazine were granted Canadian status several decades ago under R.S.C. 1952, and are, by law, Canadian publications with inherited responsibilities and rights.
One of the rights, under the Canadian Bill of Rights, 1960, part 1, section (b), is the right to equality of the law and the protection of the law.
The law is defined under part II, section (2) of the act to mean an Act of the Parliament of Canada, enacted before or after the coming into force of the act, any order, rule, or regulation thereunder and any law in force at the commencement of the act that may be subject to be repealed, abolished or altered by the Parliament of Canada.
In assuming authority to go beyond the law, the government has made the law a nullity.
Today the hand of power is directed against Reader's Digest and Time magazine, tomorrow it could be someone else. An amendment to the Immigration Act could take away the Canadian citizenship of immigrants who have become Canadian citizens.
Another letter I received recently reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Darling:

Thank you for the information on the debates with reference to Reader's Digest and the tax policies. You certainly did everything possible to help let the Digest continue as before. We seem to be on the losing team this time, but thank you for speaking out for us.
That letter came from Mr. and Mrs. A. Baston, of Gra-venhurst, Ontario. Let us hope we are not on the losing side this time after all and that something can still be done. I am hoping that the government will yet decide to take account of the views which members of the opposition have expressed. I am speaking primarily on behalf of Reader's Digest. I know this issue was discussed and fought in committee. I know, too, that the government's own supporters are not 100 per cent in favour of the bill.
I think of certain members of the standing committee on the government side who were, in fact, against the bill. I think of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt), the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik), the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), and others. There are a great many more who may not have spoken, but those were members of the committee and they did their best to get the government to change its mind. That is one reason I am speaking in favour of the amendment recommending that the bill be given a year's hoist during which the government can reconsider its position, allowing us to consider the matter a second time.

The Secretary of State says I should inform myself. Certainly, listening to the comments made by the Secretary of State and by the Minister of National Revenue it would be very hard to glean much heard information from either of them. I think the most important thing, watching the performance of the Minister of National Revenue today, was to see how he reversed himself on the policy. He has decided, in an arbitrary fashion, to interpret the legislation in a very different way from the way he said earlier he would be interpreting it. Now, apparently, Reader's Digest is to stay alive.
After news release which was referred to earlier, Mr. Speaker, put out by the Reader's Digest Corporation, they heaved an audible sigh of relief about the fact that the government had reversed itself and felt there could not be an accommodation between Reader's Digest and the Minister of National Revenue. Mr. Speaker, before Reader's Digest feels too comfortable in its new position, before it feels its future is assured, it should take a look at the track record of this government. It should ask itself whether to trust the government to continue to support the policy which has just been announced by the minister or whether, in the erratic fashion in which it has been acting today, the government is not apt to reverse itself again in the future.
The government has been legislating by interpretation in this matter. Then make quite clear what they want to do, and then they find some way around the law without even coming before parliament-as in the case of the 80 per cent difference provision-and thus find some way to force their will upon parliament and the Canadian people. When it suits their purposes to do so, Mr. Speaker, they can keep on flipping back and forth, and it may be that Reader's Digest will find once again that they are put on the firing line. They should be aware of this and should look critically at the behaviour of the government before the standing committee.
The Secretary of State, when he spoke earlier, talked of the very open nature of the proceedings before the committee and of the debate which we have carried on in connection with this piece of legislation. Mr. Speaker, if the proceedings in the committee were an example of openness and of the government's perception of the way in which legislation should be handled, I fear for this country's future. I think what has happened in this parliament, and what was exemplified very well by the government's behaviour in the committee as this bill was being studied, is that the government has proven itself to be contemptuous of the rights of parliament and contemptuous of the rights of the Canadian people. They did not have any time for dissent on this bill. The minister himself is very intol-

erant of people who express opinions which differ from his own. He made that clear in his remarks today. He just wants to put this legislation through, no matter how people feel.
If you take a look at the government's behaviour in committee you will see it has followed a course of action, which I think is very dangerous, in saying that there would be a time limit put on the debate in the committee whether the committee members liked it or not. The government said there was a time limit by which the bill would have to be reported back to the House of Commons, and that the government would put it through the House whether we liked it or not.
At that committee there were a number of Liberal members who had the courage of their convictions to stand up and say they disagreed with the position taken by the government, that they felt this was bad legislation and should not be passed. How were they rewarded for that courage? Let us take the case of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), the former chairman of the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts. I had the honour in the last parliament to serve on that committee under his chairmanship and I feel he was a very excellent chairman. He was one member of the Liberal caucus who stood and said that in his judgment this was bad legislation. He had the courage to do that in spite of the fact that the government does not look very kindly upon people who speak their own minds. What happened to him? He was not allowed to speak by the Liberal members.
The only way in which a Liberal member who disagrees with government policy can be allowed to speak before a committee is by that member going to the opposition and asking for opposition time to speak.

I think when the publishers of Reader's Digest issue news releases and applaud the course of direction taken by the government they should take a look at the government's track record and the government's erratic behaviour to date. They should take a look at the way the government views those who dissent in respect of government decisions, and they should fear for their future as a publishing entity in Canada.
The minister's problem with this bill is not that he is faced with opposition from this side of the House or that we have been unreasonable in any way in our dealings with the bill. The problem is that the minister has handled the bill in a very incompetent fashion. This piece of legislation is the bright, shining epitome of the government's approach toward the problems of periodicals in Canada.
I asked the minister during the second reading debate, and I ask him again now, when will the government be introducing a Canadian periodicals policy? What is the government's policy in respect of Canadian publishing? We know what it is. It is to continue the vendetta against Time and Reader's Digest, and I do not think that is acceptable in Canada today.

February 3, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
The members on this side of the House feel very strongly that positive action should be taken to encourage the growth, the health, and the vitality of the Canadian periodicals industry. The minister has done nothing to encourage or sustain the vitality of that industry. Before the minister forces this legislation through the House and puts this piece of punitive legislation into effect we should be able to give him time to reconsider his policies and present parliament with a Canadian periodicals policy which will give positive incentive to Canadian publishers.
I am pleased to see that Maclean's magazine has decided to go bi-weekly and become a news magazine. This is a healthy development in Canada and I applaud it. No member on this side of the House would in any way want to denigrate the development that has taken place. I do not know of any member on this side who would want in any way to discourage the development of new Canadian periodicals which are spoken of from time to time in these debates. None of us would want to discourage the development of a truly indigenous Canadian news magazine.
The minister in answer to questioning at the committee by myself, I believe last summer or spring, indicated that there were at least two or three groups looking at the possibility of establishing a new Canadian news weekly. Where are these groups? They have not surfaced. We have not seen an indication that if we drive Time of Canada out of business we will in fact have a wholly new Canadian news weekly. I think it is incumbent upon the minister, before he forces this legislation through parliament, to tell us what groups there are at the present time which have made a firm commitment to establish a new Canadian news weekly, and we would like to see this. We would also like to be able to have the opportunity of questioning the minister on the positive incentives he is giving to groups to form news weekly publications in Canada.
What is at issue here is really the right of Canadians to read what they want to read. Certainly it was made clear to me over the course of the Christmas recess that Canadians resent the increasing government involvement in their day-to-day lives. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) perhaps does not, and he has told us it is going to be necessary for even greater government control of our day-to-day activities.
Canadians who for many years have supported Canadian Time and Reader's Digest are asking for nothing more than the opportunity to continue as they have in the past to read the periodicals they enjoy. The government, for some inexplicable reason, is anxious to deprive them of that right. That is a wrong and disastrous course of action for the government to be following at this time.
If Reader's Digest can survive, as it has indicated today in its news release, this is very interesting because the government will have admitted defeat on one of the things it wanted to do. It is quite clear, if you read speech after speech made by government members on second reading of this bill, that they were anxious to do away with Reader's Digest in Canada, and did not like the sort of service provided Canadians by Time Magazine. It is quite clear in this case, if what Reader's Digest says is correct, that at least in respect of Reader's Digest the government has admitted defeat and decided that Reader's Digest should be allowed to continue. This is one very important develop-
ment that has taken place today. The government has retreated on one aspect of this bill.
This whole issue raises questions of economic and cultural nationalism. I believe we should do whatever we can to repatriate our economy and culture to Canada. I believe this should be done by strong, positive incentives which will allow Canadians to encourage entrepreneurship. I am sure that Canadians would support the government in passing legislation which sets rules of behaviour for corporations operating in Canada, and I believe that multinational corporations operating in Canada are willing to accept that. Some of the argument that has been made in respect of this legislation is that this is precisely what the government is doing. I do not think that is the case.
A couple of years ago the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and I had the opportunity of travelling to Washington and talking to the people there who run the Canadian desk in the U.S. State Department. We asked them about this question of economic and cultural nationalism, and what American reaction, both governmental and of the business community, was to Canadian action attempting to Canadianize our economy. I was surprised by the response. I had initially expected there would be a certain amount of hostility among Americans to a Canadian attempt to take control of our own economy. I was surprised to learn that was not the case.
The official with whom I spoke stressed the fact that Americans recognize that we must be the masters in our own house. They recognize the fact that Canadian nationalism and Canadian independence are a healthy force in the world today. They recognize it is necessary and quite proper that we should take action to protect our interests and to encourage Canadian culture.
These people made the point very clearly that they were prepared to live with whatever rules were set by the Canadian government. They felt that the American business community was willing to abide by these rules. However, they pleaded with us that, once we set the standards for American corporations operating in Canada, we live up to our own regulations. They cited instances where the government had simply reversed itself overnight; having set standards of behaviour for Americans operating in Canada it changed the rules in the middle of the game. This is clearly the case in respect of this legislation.
The government has brought in legislation before. At the present time there are regulations governing the conduct of Reader's Digest in Canada. For some unknown reason the minister has decided it is not good enough that they abide by the laws which have been passed by the Parliament of Canada, and not good enough that they attempt to be good corporate citizens in following the regulations which were set by the government from time to time. Now he wants to do away with these companies operating in Canada.
This is the sort of reversal or flip-flop on the part of the government that has done so much damage to our relations with our neighbours to the south. Those people recognize and accept the concept that Canadians should take strong action to repatriate control over our own economy, but they say that once we set the rules and pass the legislation in this parliament, and once we say to foreigners that they are welcome to operate in Canada as long as they abide by
February 3, 1976

our regulations and our laws here, we should stop flip-flopping overnight and completely reversing ourselves. I think Canadians, and the other people who would like to operate in this country, are entitled to better behaviour on the part of our government.
Before Christmas the hon. member for Frontenac-Len-nox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack) raised another point at which I think we should take a look. I refer to the effect the government's action will have on the stock of Reader's Digest. The people who have invested in the stock will find that their equity has turned down because of the government's action. I think many Canadians, who are not rich or powerful, are trying to save for retirement by investing in such a company. The action of the government simply will take away a part of the nest egg they have been trying to set up for their retirement. I think this is a point which should be recognized by the government.
I repeat that this bill is not in the interest of the Canadian public and industry. The government is proven to be bankrupt when it comes to producing incentives for Canadians to develop a strong and viable publishing industry in Canada.
The minister has lost the respect of the Canadian cultural industry. He has been forced to go incognito with his new beard so that he will not be recognized by angry artists who are tired of the vacillation they see today. I think members on this side of the House feel very strongly that the government has a responsibility to come up with strong, positive policies to encourage Canadian cultural nationalism and give the artistic community an opportunity to survive and prosper. This legislation does not do that. It is punitive, unfair, and bad legislation. I believe this legislation should be set aside for another year before it is put into effect.

Mr. Speaker, there are a few things I should like to say about this legislation at this point in time. It seems to have a tendency to degrade this institution and the people in it by leaving the impression with the public that members of parliament do not have a voice and are not heard, but I think the fact that members of parliament in all corners of this House have expressed some of the reactions of the Canadian public shows that we do have a concern and speak out about that concern on our own part and on the part of our constituents.
I believe the public has taken some heart from the fact that spokesmen from all parts of this House have expressed their views in the hope that perhaps the government would respond. While I am not completely happy about the way in which the government has responded, I should say that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) at the very least has ears that hear, and has a public perception of what people want, as well as an appreciation that perhaps culture cannot be legislated or that social habits cannot be legislated, as some of his colleagues unfortunately seem to believe.
From that point of view I always feel it is great when parliament is strengthened in any way and when members of parliament, regardless of their political affiliations,
Non-Canadian Publications
stand up and are counted on behalf of their constituents. In that regard I would have to say the ruling in respect of the regulations indicated by the minister is a victory for the individual member of parliament in this Chamber.
Second, I should like to say that unfortunately, as so often happens, once again the deliberations of the committees associated with this parliament have been proven to be useless and worthless from the point of view of really producing something of value and benefit to the Chamber. Committees are asked to consider in depth the legislation that is placed before the House. Witnesses are invited from all parts of the nation to appear before committees to express their views. Then in some minister's office negotiations are carried out that are not heard by members of the committee and that are not a part of the report rendered by the committee.
The government made a farce of the committee which considered this legislation by moving members in and out of it in a game of musical chairs when it was found that some members voiced dissent in respect of the government's proposals. Then at the eleventh hour the people affected sat down with the minister and his officials, and all of a sudden a magic formula appears which changes the whole concept of what the legislation is purported to do. That, unfortunately, is the bad aspect of parliament and what it stands for; it is a bad aspect of the committee system so far as this parliament is concerned.
I remember an occasion when the Standing Committee on National Defence was supposed to be considering what our posture would be in respect of NATO. In the midst of our hearings the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a pronouncement which did not even take into account the fact that the committee was deliberating on the matter. He cut them off at the pass concerning what they might produce. How can members of parliament take committees seriously when this happens time and time again when the committees are considering propositions that have been placed before them? That is the sad part of what has happened today.
What bothers me, my leader, and most members who are taking part in the debate on this subject is that here we have a firm that is in the business of publishing which has a deep concern about what its future in this nation would be if the legislation should become effective, whose representatives find themselves in the unfortunate position of going to a minister's office and accepting a proposition in relation to regulations as to the future of their operations.
I have no doubt that the Minister of National Revenue is as good as his word. He always has been with me and in this House. I am sure he will always be so long as he is a member of this House, either in cabinet or outside cabinet. I know that any businessman who had to rely on what this minister told him could feel confident about the word of the minister, but I am very concerned about the fact that he might not always be the Minister of National Revenue. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on November 24, 1975, the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) spoke at the opening of the CBC centre in Vancouver, and toward the end of his remarks he had this to say about Bill C-58, which is really his latest pronouncement: "At this time I cannot say how effective the legislation will be. We will have to give it time." Unfortunately the bill has not had time to be passed, to be brought into being or to work, let alone to become established.
We cannot demand a guarantee of success every time the government brings in legislation, and we do not in this case. However, while guarantees are unnecessary, surely there should be some likelihood of success before the government asks this House to approve a measure such as this. I suggest to the minister that there is no such likelihood in the case of Bill C-58. On what basis do I make this suggestion? I make this suggestion having sat on the committee and heard, time and time again, from witness after witness that Bill C-58 cannot and will not achieve what it was set up to accomplish.
What seems to be the purpose of this measure? It seems that the purpose of this measure at many different levels, and from perhaps even the smaller, more insignificant level, is just taxation, and it applies to the larger and broader issues of Canadian cultural identity, Canadianism and so forth. I wish to address myself to that element a little later on, but first I should like to outline some of the other reasoning involved. It is claimed that this measure is intended to encourage the growth of a strong and viable Canadian broadcasting and publishing industry. How? It will do so by denying to all advertisers in non-Canadian media the right to deduct the cost of such advertising from income tax as a business expense.
Since this bill has received second reading I cannot reiterate my opinion that it is unfortunate that the very basic principle is at fault, but because the principle is at fault, this amendment should pass. This amendment will delay implementation, and by delaying implementation perhaps the government will have an opportunity to see that a great business principle established throughout the world should be maintained in Canada.
The question is then, will this method prove successful in the stated aim of strengthening Canadian broadcasting and publishing? Again I suggest that the answer is no. Furthermore, this measure will do great damage to many Canadians, to those whose jobs will be lost and to those who may lose the reading and viewing material which has been available and which gave them a broader freedom of choice.
With regard to the potential effectiveness of Bill C-58, the first point to be made is that there is substantial evidence that no significant amounts of advertising revenue will accrue to Canadian media as a result of this measure. Of those non-Canadian media most affected, Time magazine has vowed to reduce its advertising rates to compensate its clients for the loss of tax deductibility. KVOS television in Bellingham, Washington, is going to follow the same course. Reader's Digest estimates that only 19 per cent of its current advertising would be diverted to other magazines, and most of that would go to Maclean Hunter. Now that Reader's Digest has indicated that it can
Non-Canadian Publications
reach a compromise and continue to exist under these provisions, that revenue will not accrue to Canada.
The very objective of the bill, to increase revenue to those magazines the government has defined, or seems to have difficulty defining as Canadian, and to bolster our culture as a side effect, will not be met, by the admission of the minister today in the House. So where are the massive amounts of advertising money supposedly released for the Canadian media? Where are they coming from, and how is this bill helping?
The second point to be made here was made before the standing committee by representatives of the Association of Canadian Advertisers. That is a group of 215 companies which together account for over 75 per cent of all expenditures on advertising annually in Canada. Their point is that the reduction in competition resulting from this bill could well have the inverse reaction of reducing, rather than stimulating, the demand for advertising in Canadian periodicals and on television. Mr. Tom Blakely, the president of the association, put it this way:
Our Association is concerned that if advertising expenditures cease to be deductible in circumstances contemplated by the bill, not only the purpose underlying the bill may not be achieved but also advertisers may be adversely affected.
As a lay politician I quote these people because they are expert in their field. I suggest that their knowledge is at least equal if not superior to the laymen politicians of this House. The professionals in the field tell us that we will have inverse, adverse effect rather than the positive one contemplated in the bill. Mr. Blakely also said:
Some advertisers might well reduce their expenditures in the magazine medium as a whole and use their dollars in a more efficient or less costly way.
As outlined in our position paper, Time and Reader's Digest are key factors in many advertisers' decisions to use magazines as an advertising medium. We feel that the bill would impede advertiser access to Time and Reader's Digest. Those publications may cease to publish their Canadian editions. If that happens, many advertisers would face significant cost increases in using magazines to achieve their advertising goals.
In regard to broadcasting he said:
We therefore feel that the serious reduction of border-station competition will increase the market power of the viable Canadian stations. That may result in higher advertising costs on those stations with these results. Advertisers will have to pay more for time on stations that deliver the audiences they seek and that will leave less money to be spent with new or developing stations so that, in fact, the ability of those stations to grow and become attractive to advertisers may be hindered.
Taken together these two points underline the futility of this bill. No substantial sums of money become available, and what does become available more likely than not will not end up supporting the struggling Canadian media we are supposedly trying to help. For a bill that holds out such meagre hope of yielding any positive results, C-58 has more than its share of negative end products.
It seems to me that as this bill progresses it gets in deeper and deeper. Perhaps it was well intentioned at the start but it might well be left not only for a year, as the amendments suggest, but might well be left, redrafted, and tried again under a little broader objective.

At this point I want to commend the minister, which might seem rather unusual. I think he is attempting to do something in the direction of shaping Canadian identity and I think this is a proper direction. If we look at the definition of what a Canadian is, a very simple dictionary tells us it is "a native or inhabitant of Canada". I think as maturing Canadians we need to move beyond the simple definition. I think we need to make a definition of Canadian newspapers, Canadian magazines, Canadianism and as far as the minister makes that kind of attempt in this bill,
I applaud him.
The thing that concerns me is that he seems determined to impose his idea of Canadianism upon Canada-it seems as if he feels bound to get his way and if he does not get his way he will bring in other legislation. The bill itself loses this kind of direction and credibility where we look for this Canadian identity because its first purpose becomes more and more to say yes to 75 per cent Canadian ownership. That will make it more Canadian, so I think it is a good move. But what happens after that, Mr. Speaker? The minister does not stop there but goes on to the "Canadian content different" rule.
All of a sudden what started out as a very high and worthy objective seems to move from a matter of wanting to throw out something-it starts to take on an "anti" tinge just like anti-Americanism or the evils of pro-nationalism. We have to be very careful that our pro-nationalism is not expressed in negativism. I think when we get into this content rule we go a little beyond the positive direction that was initiated in the original pronouncement of this bill.
The minister seems to be talking about Canadianism or Canadian culture. What is this elusive culture that he is attempting to stimulate by this bill? One definition defines culture as the customary beliefs, social forms, and material traits of a racial, religious or social group. The other part of that cultural identity is looked at as the condition of being the same with something described or asserted, or sameness or essential generic characteristics.
All of a sudden we are talking about losing our cultural identity, this identity of Canadianism-but we lose this anyway when in this bill we talk about content differential. If we look to this commonality of beliefs as representing a cultural identity we must ask, what is this commonality and how is it expressed? When we talk about 80 per cent difference we should really be talking about the similarities. I would suggest that between Canadian and American culture there is easily an 80 per cent similarity. In fact, I would say that would be true if comparing our culture with any other culture of mankind. We should be emphasizing the things that we have in common rather than any differences.
When we look at cultural identity I suggest that we have started a thrust here. Even if the minister scraps this bill, delays it, modifies it, or passes it, I hope he will not lose sight of this thrust, this beginning to identification of Canadianism. Indeed I hope he will carry this further because until we decide on a definition of Canadian, how can we determine how we want to get there? The first job is to identify what we are; after we identify what we are then we must decide what we would like to become, what we ought to become, and then decide on measures to work

toward this goal. We are doing it all backwards; we are feeling a strong surge of Canadian nationalism and saying, now let's do something about it, before we can even identify what it is.
I think the minister is struggling to find what it is. He talks about the struggle to uphold the ideals of Canadian identity and unity. Those are good words and thoughts, and I think he sincerely means them. The minister is a highly competent and intelligent individual and he knows that is what he was trying to do with this bill, but it is not working. I am sure he knows in his own mind that if he could accomplish only the 75 per cent Canadian ownership he would be better off than muddying the waters as he is doing with this content rule.
The content rule has much broader implications, but I do not think the minister wants a cultural czarism where we say, "This is Canadianism, and this is the border around Canada." That is what the bill is leading up to and I would ask the minister to step back and look at the amendment again. Perhaps he feels that he does not want to lose the progress the bill has made, so the bill could be referred to committee again during this year to grapple with the question of Canadian identity and culture. The subject is so large that we probably would not get near it, but we might discuss what Canadianism is, what a Canadian is, what Canadian identity is and what Canadian culture is. If we reach a common denominator on Canadian culture then we might be able to develop methods for teaching it. We are going in a directionless direction at the moment, and that needs to be changed.
My appeal on this first clause is that the minister accept this amendment and show faith in the parliamentary system, in the committee system. Otherwise this, unfortunately, will be a sad day for democracy.
The minister described the process which led to this legislation and pointed out that the government had considered, in the procedures leading to this legislation, the recommendations of two royal commissions and of the Senate committee. But he forgot to add that the parliamentary committee had also made its contribution. The parliamentary committee was engaged in its deliberations, but the minister did not allow that committee to provide any input. The government did not respond to it. Instead of listening, the minister throttled the committee and throttled his own members, so to speak. That was unfortunate for parliament and Canada, as such a committee can do a great service in establishing this country's cultural identity and showing the direction in which we should move.
I hope the minister will respond this evening and make a positive contribution. Instead of adopting a negative attitude, instead of giving a negative definition as to what a Canadian is and what Canadian culture is, let him be positive and say how we are to move positively in the direction of establishing Canadian identity. We should not move in the direction suggested by this bill.

Madam Speaker, I note that the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) listened with interest to the speech of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman). The hon. member's appeal is
February 3, 1976

valid. I hope it struck a responsive chord in the Secretary of State's mind.
The basic thrust of Bill C-58 is suspect. Frankly I fear that the government is doing again what is has done for some time past, creating an addition to its burgeoning bureaucracy. Actually I can see an entirely new bureaucracy being created. There will be new offices and new appointments, simply to monitor Canadian content. Or is the Canadian content of our Canadian publications so small that we need appoint only one person to measure it, no matter whether he measures it by column inches or percentages? That part of the Bill, I feel, is suspect. That is why I support motion No. 1, in the name of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather).
I question the ability of any thinking person to distinguish between "different", "substantially different", and "substantially the same", to distinguish between what is truly Canadian, what is pseudo-Canadian, and what is not Canadian. Apparently if a Canadian author were to write an article solely about South America or solely about Africa, his article would be classed as being of Canadian content, even though it is not about Canada. The author is Canadian you see. On the other hand, if an African author were to write an article solely about Canada, it would not be considered as being of Canadian content, because the author would be from Africa. Are these anomalies not strange? I suppose the only truly Canadian articles would be ones written by Canada's scouts or cubs. I ask hon. members to reflect on this.
Will this law, and regulations passed under it, suffer the same fate as other laws and regulations this House has passed in the last little while? For example, you will remember that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) claimed that the government was being generous with Canadians by removing the tax from shoes and clothing. Members asked if the tax saving would be passed on to the consumer and the minister said that, of course it would be; the government would monitor the process. If my memory serves me correctly, two members of this House questioned the minister at different times on the effectiveness of the program and on whether the government was making sure that the tax reduction was passed on to the consumer.
Later the government removed part of the tax on building materials and we were told that, yes, the government would monitor the process and make sure that tax savings are passed on to the consumer. That matter went into limbo. Nothing has been said about it, or heard about it. Little has been said about the tax abatement. No one, either on the government or opposition side, has expressed concern and wondered if the consumer is reaping the benefit. I suggest the same will be true with Bill C-58. Assuming it becomes law-perhaps I assume too much- and assuming the regulations are drafted, I foresee the entire matter disappearing into a vague limbo. Yes, there will be talk of monitoring the bill and of looking into the anomalies and aberrations which will take place. Finally, two or three years after passage, no one will know how to interpret the bill. That will happen if the House does not adopt motion No. 1.
The government has intruded on various aspects of Canadian life. At one time it said that the government has
Non-Canadian Publications
no place in the bedrooms of the nation. Now, apparently, it is to take its place in the reading rooms and libraries of the nation. It is to control what Canadians read. Some claim that any talk of censorship in connection with Bill C-58 is simply a red herring. I do not accept that. Surely the government is intruding on what we can read, and Lord knows for what reason. I can see the government becoming involved in other areas of our life. I should not be surprised if, next month, Playboy magazine carried in its centre fold, in full living colour, the Secretary of State in hirsute splendour, but possibly without his glasses. I don't want to get too deeply involved in this ...
That statement is a reflection of the thinking of the Secretary of State. Quite frankly, the Secretary of State has a tiger by the tail. He wishes it were a Persian cat. It is going to bite him. The minister is being scratched, indeed bloodied, by the introduction of Bill C-58.
When speaking a moment ago, the hon. member for Fraser Valley West expressed the discomfort and concerns about the areas of vagueness in this bill. I share his feelings. He asked where the minister is heading and what he truly wants.
In the treatment of this bill in this House, there has been very unusual procedure. It was forced into closure on second reading, expanded and debated in committee at great length, and four members of the government party were removed from the committee. I am sure Your Honour will agree that that is an unusual procedure.
With the protracted debate on clause 1, it is very difficult to conceive that in the beginning the bill probably had wide Canadian support. Letters from my constituency run ten to one in opposition to the position of the minister. That is a reversal of feeling. Why is it present? It is because of its vagueness of basic purpose, and its thrust which is really no longer understood by Canadians, nor for that matter by many members of this House.

There are three points that can best be made at this time with reference to an organization called the B.C. Civil Liberties Association. In a letter addressed to the minister that association said, and I quote:
Unfortunately, we cannot consider the promotion of a 'truly Canadian' outlook by the destruction of what have hitherto been publications supported by Canadian readers as other than censorship. Censorship in our understanding is content control or content manipulation by government.
This is a very unusual, perhaps unexpected approach by the B.C. Civil Liberties Association which, like any other organization of similar thrust, is nationalistic in its views. It went on to say:
Deduction of expenses does not appear to us to be a privilege which the government of the day has allowed a business only where socially desirable aims are to be achieved by the outlay. Deductibility is the ordinary rule and not a 'special advantage'... thus the content test which may result in non-deductibility for advertising in certain publications (which may be domestically owned and printed) creates an anomaly operating against these publications. It does not remove an anomaly which once favored them.
In their final remarks they stated:
We do not know what aspect of content a future government, still disclaiming (as you do) any intention to censor, might see fit to consider in imposing taxation. A still more nationalistic administration might decide to define only writings about Canada as domestic for taxation purposes.
A paternalistic government might decide that creation of jobs for Canadian writers was so high a priority that only Canadian citizens' work would rank as domestic. As civil libertarians, we would not be concerned with what laudable motives might underlie either of these fears of content manipulation.
Nor are we concerned with the policy of cultural renaissance which underlies the current government's policy. Our objection is to the intended results, not to the reason for seeking those results.
So spake the B.C. Civil Liberties Association. I would think that the directors of that organization in seeing the letter go forward would certainly be aware of its contents and be prepared to endorse them. Otherwise it would never have gone forward. It is interesting to note that among the directors of the B.C. Civil Liberties Association we find such notables as "Justice Minister Ron Basford". The party to my left, which is in favour of Bill C-58, has failed to mention this, but another of the directors of the B.C. Civil Liberties Association, and his name is given, is the great libertarian, Tommy Douglas. Is it not strange that we should have two such notable politicians who in the House are supporting the bill and who serve as directors of an association which strongly opposes it?
My other concern is with reference to the very thrust of the 80 per cent, 75 per cent, 20 per cent, 40 per cent, or whatever. There is nothing in the bill that really defines it. We have been informed that these provisions will appear in the regulations. I understand the second amendment will deal with that very fact. However, I find it very disturbing that it is not clearly spelled out in the bill. Rather, it is subject to the whim and change of the ever-changing ministers. God knows, we see enough of that in this House. It is also subject to the ever-changing bureaucrats who perhaps will be responsible for the implementation of Bill C-58 if and when it becomes law.
Let me join with other members of the House such as the hon. member for Fraser Valley West in supporting amendment No. 1 at report stage of Bill C-58.

speechtext:
I guess those Phillistines opposite do not recognize good poets when they hear them.
It has always been the hallmark of good journalism that information should have free concourse in a society. The free interaction of information and discussion has always been the accepted medium of discovering truth, and truth has always been the goal of good journalism. It is upon the percolation of information and discussion that news magazines and the intellectual health of a nation depend. Now, it would seem, those famous lines must be rewritten on the basis of the government's intention, and we must read them:
On a huge hill,
Cragged and steep, truth stands, and he that will Reach her, about must, and about must go To the Secretary of State's Department,
The Revenue Department and the Justice Department.
I suggest this is not the kind of foundation on which a nation is built, and I would simply refer to the historic experiences of nations around the world which have experienced the kind of measures the government is trying to introduce. If the government would look at the historical record of those nations which have introduced measures such as this, which really has at its heart the control of free access to information, it would find that the nations which introduced such legislation are those with which it would not want to identify itself.
Look through the pages of history at the experience of the nation of Persia or of the nation of Rome. Look at the Reformation and the Counter-Reformation. Now look at the 17th century in England. It was a Puritan government in England which first introduced legislation requiring the licensing of books in that country. The government felt legislation was necessary to control information because it was not sure what the printers were going to print and wanted to make sure that the material that went out to the reading public would meet the desires of the establishment of the day-that it would no way threaten those in power. I keep wondering whether there is a parallel between the experience of those nations and the government we face today.
Behind all this, I suggest, is a feeling of insecurity. Surely when we begin to build walls we are announcing in loud terms that we feel insecure, that we feel threatened. One of the hon. members opposite has already used a very good term for it, namely, cultural paranoia. Maybe the government is experiencing just that. It feels threatened from every side.
It seems strange to me that while the government is seeking to impose restrictions of this nature on the pub-
Non-Canadian Publications
lishing industry it should also be espousing the cause of free enterprise-at least it was doing so as recently as last December. Until last December, at any rate, the market was to be open. On one hand they want a free market in the economy but, on the other, they do not want a free market place in the publishing industry, in the world of ideas. What is wrong? Is something wrong with the thought patterns of Canadians? Is there something wrong with the way we think? Is there something wrong about the ideas which come across international boundaries? Are we afraid of those ideas?
Along with all other members of the House I want to see the Canadian identity enhanced, and in many ways I agree we are sometimes too greatly affected by cultures other than our own. But that is a choice we make. We can never reach the point in this country at which we restrict our people when it comes to opportunities to make an individual choice. As soon as we restrict free movement of ideas across international boundaries we are telling the people: you do not have the right to choose what you should read or think.
While I enjoy the distinctiveness of the Canadian identity I hasten to add that I do not regard it as sacred. It is not the only valid identity in this world. Are we afraid of the ideas which come from the United States, or of the ideas which may come from Germany, Japan, India or China? Why is it the government wants to restrict the 80 per cent content on the free inflow of information? I ask the minister very seriously whether members of his department or any other department of government are competent to deal with this kind of legislation?
The issue is not one of establishing a Canadian publishing industry. The issue is whether each Canadian has the right to read that literature he chooses to read, and make for himself the decisions as to what reading material ought to cross his desk. Again we come to the same issue on the other side of the spectrum. We are dealing with periodicals that for the most part are widely accepted across Canada as being reputable, wholesome reading literature, albeit in the case of Time magazine especially we may not always agree with its opinions as it may have some subtle overtones. At least we have the opportunity of making the decision. What the government wants to do now is take that choice away from us.
The decision on the part of the government to introduce a content rule is restrictive and paranoic, and has no place in a country that honors freedom. As I have suggested before, if the government is really serious about having dependable guidelines, and I emphasize the word dependable, for writers to follow, the most simple thing the government can do is withdraw this legislation as it stands and include the so-called Cullen rule, so that the country will then know in a very firm way exactly where we stand on this ruling, and will not be carried about on the whim of fancy of every minister who comes into this portfolio. The rule will then not be subject to the dyspepsia, of the minister of the day.
How are we going to know whether the departmental rule which says 80 per cent today is going to mean 80 per cent tomorrow? Our country is founded on law and on the

need for a firm and dependable understanding of where we are. I challenge this minister to find some way of including his ruling in the law so that we know by the final decision of this House that we are dealing with a statute and not with a departmental regulation.

Madam Speaker, I thought we were discussing motions Nos. 2 and 3 at the same time. I was suggesting that the amendment I proposed was a very simple one which requires little explanation. It would exempt from the changes the minister has proposed newspapers or periodicals whose general content relates to scientific or medical subjects published in the general interest of and for the benefit of professionals. My amendment deals with a very specific type of printed material which zeroes in on subjects of particular and specific interest to professionals and scientific people. I cannot for the life of me think why such scientific material would represent any sort of challenge to the cultural integrity referred to in this bill.
If the material to which I refer does not in any way affect the culture of Canada and is rather strongly directed towards scientific and medical material, I can see absolutely no objection, and no reason why we should not exempt that type of published material.
It has been said that the government does not want to make any exceptions. I do not understand the reason for that because I think we should not only be looking at the short term but as well at the long term in respect of these specific publications. It is already too evident that the bill seems to be pointing at two publications, namely, Time and Reader's Digest. We have all seen the statement of Mr. Zimmerman on behalf of Reader's Digest this afternoon. It seems to me that if we are going to consider this legislation we should have the wisdom to adopt the long-term view, and in that way present acceptable legislation. In this way we would not be placing unacceptable controls on the publication of specific scientific and medical material which is published for the purpose of educating doctors and scientists. I certainly hope this House will give favourable consideration to this amendment, finding it desirable and acceptable.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Cullen (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I listened to the speaker for the opposition, just prior to the last speaker, I wondered whether we were even talking about the same bill. There seemed to be some suggestion of censorship, or that people are being forbidden to read what they choose to read. I would respectfully suggest another reading of the bill which would indicate that there is freedom of information, and a freedom of choice so that the Reader's Digest, Time, or any other material the hon. member wants to read will still in fact be available.
I think this kind of misrepresentation and misstatement in respect of the bill does the hon. member little credit and does a disservice to the Canadian public. There is in fact no intention to curtail the free flow of information. I will leave it at that, and deal primarily with the percentage content.
It seems to me as we reach this stage of the bill it would be appropriate that I make a few comments on the government's interpretation of "substantially the same" as used in Section 19 of the Income Tax Act. The interpretation has been both misunderstood and misrepresented, and I welcome this opportunity to ensure that the record is clear.
On January 23, 1975, the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) announced the government's intention to remove the special tax status enjoyed by certain foreign-controlled publications. Bill C-58 seeks to repeal sub-sections 19(2) and 19(4) of the Income Tax Act, and in that way no business deduction may be claimed for the cost of an advertisement placed in an issue of a non-Canadian periodical if the particular advertisement is directed primarily to a market in Canada.
Predictably and appropriately enough, periodicals affected by this change in legislation carefully re-examined the bill first passed in 1965 and had little difficulty in understanding that in order to become qualified as a Canadian magazine within the meaning of the act it would become necessary first to be produced and published in Canada.
Second, it would have to be 75 per cent owned and controlled in Canada. Third, it should not be produced under some licensing arrangement with another magazine.
The fourth criterion, that is, that the contents must not be substantially the same as those of a foreign periodical, has not been as clearly understood and has needed clarification. I think it is fair to say that estimates of the required degree of difference ran from 50 per cent to over 80 per cent, and we have heard as high as 100 per cent. It had been the intention of my predecessor in office to announce the interpretation to be given those words at the committee stage. However, because the effective date in the bill was January 1, 1976, I felt it was more appropriate to make my decision, and to make it known, as soon as possible so that publishers and advertisers would be aware of their tax positions and have an opportunity to rearrange their affairs accordingly.
In deciding the interpretation to be given to the words "not substantially the same", there were several criteria to be followed. First and foremost, the government's intention was clear: there were to be no special privileges or exemptions under section 19(1) of the Income Tax Act. I
February 3, 1976

should point out at this point that such a position was a recommendation of two federal inquiries, the Royal Commission on Publications, which has been called the O'Leary Commission, and the special Senate Committee on the Mass Media. The thrust of both inquiries was that exemptions granted to foreign publications under income tax legislation should be repealed to ensure the survival of a healthy indigenous periodical industry.
To give effect to the government's intention, it was obvious that a specific position had to be determined. Secondly, the provision relating to "substantially the same" was enacted in 1965 so that Canadian publications would not have undue competition for advertisers from "split runs" or "dressed up" versions of foreign publications. The requirements with respect to ownership and control by Canadian citizens, that is, 75 per cent, and the preclusion of licensing agreements, made it obvious that a great measure of independence would be expected from a truly Canadian periodical.
With this in mind I issued a press release on October 23 to announce that, in order to be considered not substantially the same as one or more issues of one or more foreign periodicals, more than 80 per cent of the contents of a Canadian periodical must be material which has not appeared in any current or prior issue of foreign publications with which the Canadian periodical has any type of continuing arrangement for access to material.
There has been some criticism of the procedure because this is, after all, an interpretation. Quite frankly I would have preferred an amendment to the Income Tax Act to specify unequivocally that the words "not substantially the same" be defined by regulation as meaning 80 per cent different. However, this would require a new notice of ways and means motion, and such an amendment would not be feasible at this time.
I have met personally with Mr. Paul Zimmerman of Reader's Digest and his counsel, and also with Mr. LaRue of Time Canada and his counsel, together with a counsel from one of the intended purchasers, indicating that my announcement, like thousands of others we are called upon to make, was an interpretation. However, because it had the backing of the government and my cabinet colleagues, if a challenge were successfully made it would be incumbent upon the government to proceed under a new notice of ways and means motion to define the meaning of the words, to restore the government's intention.
This has been the subject of some criticism and I would like to comment briefly upon it. First, such an amendment would not be retroactive. If an advertiser successfully challenged our interpretation in the court, that advertiser would be permitted the business deduction. My announcement about legislation that would follow a successful challenge was made as a courtesy to those who might see fit to launch an action and spend a considerable amount of money-only to find that down the road the policy's intent would be restored by legislation. This procedure of subsequently amending legislation is not unprecedented.
Usually when parliament passes legislation it announces the intention of that legislation, and what it is proposed to do. Sometimes that legislation is challenged, loopholes are discovered, or court decisions are rendered that are different from the original intent of parliament. When this
Non-Canadian Publications
happens, future legislation is passed to plug the loopholes, or to give effect to the original intention. I submit there are many precedents for the introduction of such an amendment to ensure that policy intent is achieved.
In June, 1972, for example, the Department of National Revenue issued an interpretation bulletin relating to government grants to industry. In May, 1974, this interpretation was challenged before the courts, which decided in favour of the taxpayer. Because the court's interpretation of this pertinent section of the Income Tax Act did not reflect government policy, an amendment was proposed by ways and means motion in the November 18, 1974, budget. A sub-section was subsequently enacted, with effect from November 18, 1974, but not retroactive, nor is that the intention here.
In my view, public awareness of the government's intended publications policy is important, and I felt I would have been remiss in my responsibilities and been unfair to the publishing firms in question, and to their advertisers, if I had left any room for doubt that we might accept a figure less than 80 per cent. I therefore opted for letting the publishing industry and the advertisers know well in advance precisely what the government's intention was.
The reference to "continuing arrangement" in the press release is vital to the understanding of our interpretation of "substantially the same"-the written law is given much greater flexibility by its inclusion-yet it is an important point that is often missed.
Because the interpretation specifies material "acquired through a continuing arrangement" an issue of a Canadian magazine may consist of even 100 per cent "spot" articles taken from foreign periodicals and still be considered Canadian, if those articles are not obtained through a "continuing arrangement"; that is, an arrangement by which a periodical has an on-going right for availability of general material.
In the case of a digest, Mr. Speaker, the definition of continuing arrangement will not refer to that arrangement which a periodical may have with a middle party to obtain material. The purpose of the legislation is not to preclude the possibility of a digest-which, by definition, reproduces most if not all of its material existing in Canada, but rather to ensure that the editorial choice and condensation, if necessary, of that material are done in Canada.
If a continuing arrangement must be made through a second party to have access to third party material, it would not be the purpose of the law to thwart that access but to ensure that that material is chosen and edited in Canada. The ruling remains the same. We are saying that "middle party access" used to obtain third party material will not be regarded as a continuing arrangement. This technique will allow a Canadian digest access to original material.
Before I close, Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment briefly on the recent editorial in Time magazine entitled "Freedom and Fairness". This is such a distortion of the truth and such a misleading representation of the facts that it simply cannot go unanswered.

I take strong issue with the suggestion that my department or my predecessor misled Time. The former minister indicated in early discussions with Time editors that a content decision had not been made-that this would have to be referred to cabinet. He assured Time editors that this would not be less than 50 per cent, but at no time did he suggest that it would be 50 per cent.
The only public declaration made by the former minister with regard to content was that somewhere between 60 per cent and 80 per cent would have to be different content to qualify for the definition of "Canadian". The memo referred to in the Time editorial was part of a draft memo, never sent and never signed. It had been prepared with regard to format. No particular attention was being given at that time to the question of content. Time lawyers and editors know this as well as anyone and have twisted the words ripped from an unsent, unsigned memo to suit their own purposes. This is misrepresentation of the worst order.
In fact declaring that the government's policy requires that more than 80 per cent of the contents of a Canadian periodical must be material which has not appeared in any current or prior issues of foreign publications with which the Canadian periodical may have any type of continuing arrangement for access to material, allows more, not less freedom to periodicals. Articles do not have to have Canadian subjects, nor be written by Canadian authors. Canadian magazines will have access to a variety of foreign sources and still qualify as a Canadian magazine, as long as there is no continuing arrangement with the source for more than 20 per cent of their material.
The 80 per cent content ruling does not abridge, check or change the free flow of any information. Foreign magazines should and will continue to appear on all newsstand-but alongside their issues will be stronger and better Canadian periodicals which will be benefiting from a redirection of Canadian advertising support. This is the intent of Bill C-58.

This interpretation was arrived at through much careful consideration of the interests involved. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I simply wish to direct the attention of the House to one point. Quite frankly I alluded to it this afternoon.

I rise tonight because I find the attitude of the government completely shocking. I am not speaking now about the policy of 80 per cent difference or any policy. I am referring rather to the fact that the parliament of Canada has passed a statute which, like other statutes, would normally be interpreted by the courts in case of any dispute. We are now being asked to adopt an amendment to that statute, and we are being told simultaneously by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) what "substantially different" means. I want to know what there is in any statute and any tradition in this country that gives a minister of the Crown the right to determine authoritatively, and without reference to the courts, what the words of acts of parliament mean. Who gave the Minister of National Revenue the authority to determine what "substantially different" means? It is a complete usurpation of the position of our courts in this country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS

I find it completely revolting that the government should take an existing statute, introduce an amendment, and then say how that statute passed some ten years ago will in fact be interpreted, regardless of what a court may say as to what "substantially different" means. Courts are not to be allowed to determine whether "substantially different" means 80 per cent different.
The minister referred to a ruling he has given arising out of conversations with representatives of Reader's Digest about the importance of the existence or the lack of a continuing arrangement. Is that in a statute? Is there anything in our statutes about continuing arrangements? Is there anything in the statutes passed by this parliament, or which we are asked to pass, which relates continuing arrangements or the absence of them to "substantially different"? I ask that question.
There is nothing in the statute which we are asked to pass which gives the Minister of National Revenue, or indeed the governor in council, the authority to say that the absence of a continuing arrangement as he defined it is significant or determinant for this purpose.
I rise at this time, as I say, not in connection with the policy at all but to express my distate for and indeed disgust with the approach of the government which in effect removes the whole question of interpretation of the statutes from the courts. I would like some member of the government to set my mind at rest or to point out to me if I am wrong in this respect.
I say it is a complete subversion of our whole judicial system. I do not see how the government and its supporters can ask this parliament to endorse a proposal or an approach which takes away from the courts the interpretation of statutes already passed by this legislature and substitutes the Minister of National Revenue as the Supreme Court of Canada in this respect, without the slightest authorization by parliament.
The minister says that he is trying to be helpful by telling publishers and others how the statute will in fact be interpreted by the department. I suggest to the minister that neither he nor his colleagues have that kind of an authority, and if I am wrong, if I misunderstood the situation, I would like to be corrected. It seems to me that the government, in an entirely arbitrary way, is assuming the
February 3, 1976

right to interpret in a manner beyond appeal what the words of parliament mean, and that is something that I am not prepared to accept, quite apart from any question of policy.

In any event, as I pointed out at the beginning, aside from wanting to make a brief comment with respect to the comments of the Leader of the Opposition, I really want to deal more substantively, but briefly, with motion No. 3, which has been brought forward by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy). This amendment would provide an exemption for periodicals which deal with scientific or medical subjects. In that respect I must say that on June 4, 1975, in the second reading debate on this bill I raised for the first time the question of Modern Medicine, MD of Canada, and some possible other publications in that caterogy. At that time I indicated that I felt it was unacceptable that we prepared legislation in such a way that it would prohibit our people in the medical field from having access to whatever information may be available form elsewhere in the world.
It can be argued that these magazines can be published in the United States, printed there, forwarded into Canada and our medical people could have access to those journals, and I agree that that is a valid argument. Nonetheless, we should bear in mind that the stated purpose of this bill- and there may be a difference between what is stated and what is perceived to be the purpose-is to assist Canadian publishing concerns, and to that I largely subscribe. I think most of us, if not all of us, would like to see a healthy publishing industry in Canada, so we do not disagree with that. However, with respect to this motion I should like to raise one point.
How indeed are we going to help the publishing industry in Canada by effectively prohibiting under previous conditions the right to publish Md of Canada or Modern Medicine in Canada? Do they have competitors in Canada to which the advertising would be diverted? To my knowledge, the answer is no. Are we really suggesting that those who advertise in publications do so on a willy nilly basis?

Therefore, if we want to assist the magazine industry in this country substantially, it seems to me that we must deal with two aspects; first, attack the dumping problem. If there is editorial material coming into Canada at a price to the Canadian publisher or subsidiary of a foreign publisher in Canada at a cheaper rate than they could generate it themselves, we should deal with that kind of question in ordinary, traditional ways through our dumping legislation, and that appears to be the appropriate way to deal with that aspect of the question.
Second, if we really want to help the magazine industry in Canada, we need more advertising dollars directed into periodical publications as opposed to other advertising media. When we consider this side of the coin, it is quite evident that Canada has one of the lowest rates of advertising per advertising dollar in the publication industry in the world. Less than half our advertising dollars are diverted to the magazine industry in comparison with the United States. We are so far below that which occurs in Europe that it is almost beyond description.
For instance, I understand that in Italy something over 50 per cent of every advertising dollar goes to the periodical industry. In Germany, France, and England there are very large percentages compared with that of Canada which, I believe, is in the neighbourhood of 2.8 per cent.
If we really think that we ought to protect, expand and to give reason for new Canadian magazines to come into the field, perhaps we ought to consider this matter altogether differently, and we ought to indicate to advertisers that if they want a tax advantage from advertising in Canada, they should divert at least 5 per cent of their advertising dollars into the periodical industry. By doing so we would have twice the advertising revenue and many more Canadian magazines. That would be a very constructive approach to assisting the magazine industry. The present approach, particularly as it relates to this amendment, is not productive in terms of helping anybody in the magazine industry. It will simply adversely affect two medical journals which provide information to our doctors and professionals in this country. I frankly, am prepared to vote in favour of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Timmins.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) and what he had to say, as well as the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) who, in my view, put the situation in its proper light.
As we know, the Canadian population today has reached about 221/2 million people. We also know that medical science extends around the world. Experimental work is being done in China, in Great Britain, in France, in Ger-

many, in the United States, South America-all over the world. The Canadian magazines in the medical field that the hon. member for Ontario mentioned, Modern Medicine and M.D. of Canada, come in free to the medical profession, bringing the latest scientific data gathered from all over the world.
I think it would be the height of folly to build a wall and say that we have all the scientific expertise we need in this country. We know what would happen to the exchange of ideas in the medical field then. Just to give an example, the Mayo clinic is doing research work on dissolving gallstones. A Canadian firm and others are also working in this field. When the research is complete it will be available to medical periodicals all over the world, not only for the benefit of the United States but that of the world at large. If there is humanity in this parliament how can we deny this information to countries that are ill-equipped and cannot afford the research?
Only a few years ago Great Britain was the medical centre of the world, but the centre has now shifted to the United States. We are doing a lot of valuable research work in Canada because of our connections and communications through journals and other ways with the United States. In the field of aeronautical science we are learning about the reaction of the human body in the medical end of that speciality and this knowledge is made available to the world through the magazines that I have mentioned. Knowledge about operative procedures in the same field is made available as well.
It is interesting that the hon. member for Ontario said that if we want to publish magazines in Canada the first thing we must do is apply for sufficient funds or get people to advertise in these journals. That is not the case at the moment; advertisers are using other avenues. I think the figures that the hon. member for Ontario quoted are about right. The only way these magazines can go to medical doctors, researchers, and other fields in Canada without charge is if the advertising pays for it. Modern Medicine and M.D. of Canada are well put together and bring to our attention facts that are many thousands of years old that still have a bearing on the human body.
This is the most reckless piece of legislation that I know of, Mr. Speaker. It is not only reckless, it is destructive. It is not only destructive, it is trying to build a wall to keep out information that comes to us free of charge.
I know the minister is rather a nice fellow but I cannot understand his thinking on this. He taught school himself so I cannot understand his motives. I hope he will see that this bill should be set aside for the present.
