subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to address my comments specifically to motion No. 3 standing in the name of the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy), which seeks to exempt scientific and medical periodicals from the provisions of this bill.
I should also like to reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) who, I thought, would have followed some of the testimony given in the standing committee and realized the motivation behind removing subsection 4(b) of section 19 of the Income Tax Act. I think it relates to a decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in 1972 that pointed out a loophole in the legislation that was not intended by the framers of the legislation nor by the royal commission from which the bill flowed. In order to inform the hon. member for Timmins and the hon. member for Ontario, I should like to relate some of that background and testimony. It will then become clear why the section will be repealed.
Section 19(4)(b) of the Income Tax Act exempted foreign publications from the tax effects of section 19 applying to any publication the principal function of which is the encouragement, promotion or development of the fine arts, letters, scholarship or religion. The members of the Royal Commission on Publications were clear in their intent: These foreign "little," or cultural magazines would not, I repeat, would not be carriers of Canadian advertising to Canadian audiences.
As we know, the royal commission recommended that the deduction from income tax by a taxpayer of expenditures incurred for advertising directed at the Canadian market in a foreign periodical wherever printed should be disallowed. The commission, in its conclusion and summary said that the foregoing recommendations I just mentioned would prevent the diversion of Canadian advertising expenditures from Canadian periodicals. They strike at split runs, regional editions, "Canadian" sections, "Canadian" editions, and other techniques of diversion which exist now or may be developed in future. They do not bear upon any Canadian periodicals and do not affect foreign cultural, "little," consumer or business periodicals in any way unless they are used as carriers of domestic advertising.
Non-Canadian Publications
I should mention a court case concerning JayKay Publications, which publishes a medical magazine. I will not dwell on the history of the appeal. What happened was as follows: The judge in the first instance interpreted very narrowly the question of content, but the appellate court did not look at what the judge below had considered, and looked at the total workings of the magazine. The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in 1972 meant that the courts were to interpret subsection (4) as including foreign publications used as carriers of domestic advertising. In effect it means that a loophole has been opened affecting the narrow area of educational, medical or scientific magazines.
As the law now stands as a result of the decision of the Court of Appeal, any foreign publication that can be judged to have scholarly content seems to be in the position of becoming a Canadian periodical, and any Canadian periodical that can be judged to have scholarly content could therefore be purchased by foreign interests, without subsection (1) of section 19 coming into force. This means, then, that a number of Canadian scholarly magazines in fields of medicine, history, arts, science and so on can be bought out, or foreign publications could set up equivalent magazines, under the guise of their being scholarly or scientific magazines, and these foreign publications would not be barred from using the Income Tax Act and allowing their advertisers to deduct the expenses of advertising.
The testimony we heard in committee from Canadian scholarly magazines, scientific journals, and so on, and from the Canadian Periodical Publishers' Association was to the effect that if this loophole is not plugged, which is what Bill C-58 attempts to do, Canadian magazines, especially Canadian medical publications, cannot survive the assault of this potentially new low-cost competition. Therefore I suggest it is important that this House reject motion No. 3, proposed by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy). The amendment would, if passed, open the floodgates for foreign magazines, which could qualify as scholarly or scientific publications in those narrow areas and escape the advertising prohibition provisions of the Income Tax Act.
I remind hon. members who are concerned in case this bill would somehow be a form of censorship that rejection of the amendment will not stop those magazines from crossing the Canadian border and being distributed to the scientific or medical community. Their members will still have access to those magazines. Certainly, if this bill is passed, it will protect scientific and scholarly journals of Canadian origin against unfair competition from magazines which could qualify under the loophole created by the decision in 1972 of the Federal Court of Appeal.
Let us remember that the United States has enacted much more stringent regulations concerning the publishing of scientific journals and the allowing of Canadian scientific or medical journals to penetrate tbe United States market. That may be a form of censorship or, at least, protection under American copyright legislation.
At present no foreign periodicals are denied entry to this country. Remember, this bill will not prevent them from doing so. At present Canadian scholarly publications are liable to be subject to a form of censorship, or they are

Non-Canadian Publications
denied entry to the United States by American law. Let me explain.
Unlike Canada, where our borders are open to foreign publications, the United States, through its manufacturing clause in the Copyright Act, effectively prevents Canadian journals containing articles by United States citizens from selling more than a limited number of copies in the United States without threatening the American citizen's copyright protection. The Americans do not call this censorship; they call it protecting their printing trade.
However, a Canadian publisher wishing to produce a scholarly journal concerned, for example, with medicine or economics, and to sell it to a North American market, has only two choices: to limit the size of his sale to the United States market, or to scrap the idea of including writings by American writers. No similar restriction exists in Canada, nor would Bill C-58 create such restriction.
We are in this position: the Americans, by their law, have effectively put up more barriers to the free flow of information than we have in Canada at present, or will have even after Bill C-58 passes.
For the sake of consistency, and in order to heed the intent of the royal commission, I suggest that it is important for us to reject the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Timmins. We should pass parts of the bill relating to subsection (4) and pertaining to scholarly journals as they stand. Otherwise the federal court decision which I mentioned will have opened a loophole whereby many Canadian scholarly magazines can be bought by Americans or foreign publications, and these foreign publications would then qualify for advertising advantages that were not intented for such scholarly magazines.
Also, if we do not pass the bill as is, many Canadian scholarly publications will face continued severe and unfair competition from certain magazines such as MD and others which have been able to exist through the qualifying provisions of Section 19 of the Income Tax Act. I say it is important that we do not follow or agree with the reasoning of the hon. member for Timmins or of the hon. member for Ontario.
The other point that is important and that we should turn our attention to is motion No. 2. This amendment seeks to reduce the 80 per cent substantially different clause to 50 per cent. We heard in testimony from many Canadian publishers that this would in effect destroy the intent of the legislation to promote and sustain a healthy Canadian periodical industry.
One of the great advantages that magazines like Time and Reader's Digest have that Canadian magazines do not is that those magazines can get editorial material much more cheaply from their parent companies than any competing Canadian magazine. In addition to getting that content cheaply, up until now they have been able to qualify for benefits under the Income Tax Act, or their advertisers could qualify for such benefits. This has allowed Time and Reader's Digest to capture over 50 per cent of magazine advertising revenue in this country.
If we are to agree to this amendment and reduce the substantially different aspect from 80 per cent to 50 per

cent, this will mean that magazines like Time and Reader's Digest will be able to continue to lift half of their content from parent companies outside Canada while retaining their favourable status under the Income Tax Act.
It is obvious what they will do. The 50 per cent content they can get from the parent will be the most expensive content that they will acquire. It will be the material that is before colour work, feature articles, that kind of material that Canadian companies would have severe financial difficulty trying to duplicate. They will be able to get cut-rate costs. The royal commission documented that it costs Time and Reader's Digest as little as 5 per cent of the original cost of production for these materials. It cost Canadian publications 5 per cent of the cost borne by the parent. That is a totally unfair competition for most Canadian magazines trying to work up the same material.
We accepted the opportunity of protecting Canadian industry against unfair foreign competition. I think the same principle should apply here. To reduce that content regulation would mean a windfall for these subsidiaries to get the most expensive materials at cut rates from their parent companies. It would negate the whole intent of the bill. Therefore I do not see how we can support that amendment standing in the name of the hon member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather).
I am still a bit worried about the statement of the Minister of National Revenue as to the accommodation reached with Reader's Digest on the content regulation, 80 per cent not substantially the same as the parent. As I understood him, he said there could be a continuing arrangement by the Digest with the second party in order to have access to third party sources. I would like further clarification of this. I wonder whether it does not open up a loophole for Time Canada as well in terms of the fact that Time Canada could buy original materials from Time correspondents scattered throughout the world that are in fact being subsidized by Time in the United States.
If Time Canada could buy that material at a reduced rate, or that material which is surplus to the actual material appearing in the American edition of Time, it would in effect be continuing a kind of relationship almost approaching a licensing, but different enough that these magazines could qualify as Canadian magazines for advertising income tax purposes.
If that kind of loophole exists for the Reader's Digest, and more particularly for Time, it pulls the rug out from under the intent of the legislation which is that these magazines, by virtue of their symbiotic relationship with the parent company, are not truly Canadian magazines. I want to look at Hansard tomorrow and examine very closely what the Minister of National Revenue said so that I can be very clear. Perhaps when the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) rises, he can further elaborate on that situation.
To conclude, we in the New Democratic Party cannot support motions Nos. 2 and 3 for the reasons I have outlined.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PARIS ECONOMIC CONFERENCE-POSSIBILITY OF CANADA BEING CO-CHAIRMAN-CANADIAN POSITION AT CONFERENCE
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PARIS ECONOMIC CONFERENCE-POSSIBILITY OF CANADA BEING CO-CHAIRMAN-CANADIAN POSITION AT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question dates from December 8 last when I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) whether he would put forward the ideas on trade and monetary reform to close the gap between the rich and the poor in the world, which he would be introducing at the conference on economic equality, otherwise known as the North-South Conference which was held in Paris which brought together the industrialized and the poor nations, the first real effort at bargaining on the issues which divide the rich and the poor countries. The minister replied at that time that he was then working out preliminary policy attitudes which would require elaboration as the work progressed.
Since that question was asked and the answer was given, the minister did, in fact, go to that conference in Paris, bringing honour to Canada in his role as co-chairman of the conference, and I wish to congratulate the honourable gentleman for the role he continues to play.
The conference went on into the middle of December and it was reconvened last week for two days to work out details for the work of four commissions. Canada has been appointed to two of them, namely, the commissions on energy and development.
Upon coming back to the House last week I asked the minister to give a report on the North-South Conference. The minister said he would be bringing some news of the conference before the House, perhaps this week, together with some of his own views. In his answer today he backed
Adjournment Debate
away from any commitment to bring into the House in the immediate future a report on Canada's participation in the conference, the most important conference on international life which has been held since the seventh special session of the U.N. General Assembly in September. More to the point, he backed away from his undertaking to bring before the House the policy positions to be adopted by the commissions on energy and development.
I must point out with great reluctance that the minister does not seem to be cognizant of the need to bring into a higher public profile in our country what Canada is doing in the whole application of the new international economic order with which the North-South Conference has been grappling.
While the minister was travelling overseas, I was travelling a bit myself. I went across Canada for ten days in January with two other members of parliament, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). The three of us, in a non-partisan way, sought to explain to the Canadian people why there ought to be a greater degree of Canadian participation at both government and private levels in Canada's international development program.
As we were explaining this need to the Canadian people we were constantly asked the question: what is Canada's position? Madam Speaker, the Canadian people do not know that a major shift has taken place in Canadian policy which has now been codified in the Canadian five-year strategy called Strategy for International Development Co-operation, 1975-1980. That document is not even known across Canada. That is tied in with my point tonight.
It is imperative this House be told the concrete proposals Canada is bringing before international fora at the present time-what we intend to do at the Law of the Sea Conference, what we propose to do at UNCTAD IV in Nairobi in May, as well as our continuing effort in the North-South Conference.
While all this has been going on the Canadian people are under the impression that our effort in international development is concentrated upon aid, and are not yet aware of the structural changes or the multi-dimensional policy which the five-year strategy really introduces. In the five-year strategy a commitment is made which implies a concentration of our aid upon the least developed countries, the countries now known as the fourth world, identified by the World Bank, and Canada has pledged under point 18 of that strategy to concentrate our aid on those least developed countries, about 35 in number, containing one billion people. What do we find, though?
While the minister is overseas he pledges $1 million dollars to Egypt for the rebuilding of the war-battered Suez Canal zone. Today, although he was not as cognizant of the details as we might have expected, the minister confirmed the latest announcement by CIDA of the $25 million loan in concessional terms for mutually agreed projects to Indonesia. We do not know anything about this project at all.
My point in bringing this up now in connection with the North-South Conference is that Canadian aid is going to Indonesia and to Egypt, countries which do not qualify as the least developed countries under the figures of the

February 3, 1976
Adjournment Debate
World Bank. The figures offered by the minister today show that Egypt's net per capita is income under $100, not quite in conformity with the World Bank figure which is $240. However, deplorable as that figure is, it still leaves the Canadian people in some confusion as to where our aid is going. Is it to go to the least developed countries, or are we going to continue to give aid for political purposes, whether of not those political purposes relate to our foreign policy, or is it for purposes of our trade position with Indonesia, which seems to underlie the new $25 million arrangement?
I take exception to a press release fron CIDA which attemps to explain why aid is going to Egypt, without giving any of the details. I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to bring into this House the full program of Canada's participation in international development so that we can begin to understand, with the Canadian people, some of these details, allowing us to continue our responsibilities.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-PARIS ECONOMIC CONFERENCE-POSSIBILITY OF CANADA BEING CO-CHAIRMAN-CANADIAN POSITION AT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to apologize to my colleagues in this House tonight for my unpleasant voice due to laryngitis. I should also like to thank the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Roche) for his congratulations on the role played by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Eachen) as co-chairman of the Conference on International Economic Co-Operation.
This conference has had two meetings now, as reported on by the minister not later than this afternoon in the House. I should like to clarify one thing that has been said in respect of the minister's statement as having been a "backing away", according to the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona, from his previous intention of informing the House and making a complete report on the conference in Paris.
In fact what was approved by the two chairmen, the hon. Mr. MacEachen and Manuel Perez Guerrero, of Venezuela, and the other 25 colleagues of the other countries, of which 19 are developing countries, was a timetable for meetings and a general setting of guidelines, not of policies, for the meeting of the four commissions which are to start their work on February 11.
As we know now, we are members of the energy and development commissions. We shall, of course, also be engaged in the dialogue in areas covered by the two other commissions, namely, raw materials and finance. I think it is rather easy to understand at this point in time the general strategy to be followed by the 27 members of the conference. It is to act as a team that should respect the rules of work. The 19 developing countries have indicated topics which they wish to discuss in each of the commissions. Now that this has been done we shall be indicating how we think the commissions should be working.
For instance, we have started urging the adoption of a pragmatic dialogue to avoid confrontation, and we are at this point in time urging more than what the group has been doing as a working team. It is rather interesting and difficult to launch a working team which will have to create a network of relationships and a good, positive working atmosphere in setting up the most difficult dis-

tinction between aid and trade. My colleague gave the impression of mixing the two as interchangeable, which I suggest they are not.
I do not think anyone can settle the international economic order in a few weeks. Our senior public servants reached Paris recently and are working full time on the development of the policies.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING VIEWS OF MINISTERS ON ECONOMIC POLICY-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING VIEWS OF MINISTERS ON ECONOMIC POLICY-REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is most interesting to note that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) is here this evening. I hope he is here to answer my observations personally this evening and is not here simply as an observer.
Over the past few weeks there has been considerable concern over the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) remarks on the Canadian economy. The majority of Canadians are upset, to say the least. Toronto Liberal Leaders have expressed their concern about the Prime Minister's way of fighting inflation. The former minister, the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), has requested that the Prime Minister call a Liberal caucus meeting to explain his remarks about long-term economic controls.
The president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce does not agree with the Prime Minister's remarks that the free enterprise system is not working and that we should have more government intervention. The last thing we need in this country is more government intervention.
Canada is the most over-governed country in the world both municipally, provincially, and federally. What we need is less government. The Liberal government is responsible for our economic chaos and high inflation through its uncontrolled spending which has increased 151 per cent since 1968.
Labor and unions have no faith in the government or the Anti-Inflation Board. They are organizing official protests to say they will refuse to co-operate with the government. We now have the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) clearly repudiating the Prime Minister's controversial analysis of Canada's economic system. He says he is opposed to big government and big labour. How on earth can he stay in a Liberal cabinet when he feels this way? I see him smile. He should resign immediately. The minister made the above remarks in Winnipeg recently and distributed copies of his speech to the press in Ottawa. The acting Prime Minister stated in the House last Friday that the Minister of National Defence spoke without a text in Winnipeg. This is not true, as the speech was distributed.
There is no doubt in my mind that, under the Liberals, Canada is in for permanent controls. The Anti-Inflation Board rules and regulations are becoming so complicated and involved that a huge bureaucracy will be needed to compile all the paper work that the detailed Anti-Inflation Board forms will generate.. Business is already complaining of the additional workload in its accounting systems now
February 3, 1976

that it must provide information for the Anti-Inflation Board. This in itself will add to our inflation problems.
There has never been so much confusion and concern in Canada over how we are being governed. The Prime Minister has told Canadians the choice is theirs, and he also stated he welcomes the debate about the future of Canada which the government's actions and his words have stimulated. He further stated that we are living in a new economic era. I certainly agree that the Prime Minister's remarks have stimulated debate, and if the choice of a new economic era is to be left up to Canadians then an election should be called. There could be no better time, say in May or June, as the official opposition will have a new leader in less than three weeks and this would give Canadians an opportunity to decide between Progressive Conservative policies and the Liberals' new society of more government intervention. Also, the Prime Minister claims parliament is not working well, so at this time both major parties could explain to the electorate how they would make parliament work better.
The government was not given a mandate on July 8, 1974, to introduce a three-year or permanent government control scheme. As the Liberals stated, inflation was a world-wide phenomenon and nothing could be done about it, nor was any mention made of a new economic era being introduced.
Also, when there is a split in the cabinet, and the Minister of National Defence states in his Winnipeg speech that his economic views run counter to those of the Prime Minister's, and when a former cabinet minister, the member for Windsor West, states:
that the Prime Minister's remarks have been taken by some to mean that the government is planning drastic changes in the free enterprise system and a pervasive new system of government regulationsthen I have some uneasiness about what the Prime Minister's remarks could mean. The former minister further stated:
If major changes are in store, the Prime Minister has an obligation to explain them to caucus and to the public.
This is enough in itself to warrant an election.
I also believe, Mr. Speaker, that the majority of Canadians would welcome a complete explanation from all parties as to the direction in which they would lead Canada if in power. I am also sure there would be very little objection to an election being called this spring, and under the present circumstances it would be best for the country. The parties could also explain their priorities at this time and we could have a dialogue with the Canadian public, labour, and business, as to their choice of priorities.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Public Works' (Mr. Drury) speech in Winnipeg last week on consumer buying requires clarification almost as badly as the Prime Minister's post-Christmas broadcast did. The Minister of public Works' speech also conflicts with the position now taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). His speech is also reminiscent of the disastrous Liberal policies of 1969 and 1970, of which he was a leading exponent.
Also, an election is needed so the Liberals can be more specific in their definitions of restraint and its approaches to the whole question of consumer demand. When a Liberal cabinet minister states that high consumer buying is
Adjournment Debate
harmful to Canada and is inflationary, then it is time we hit the campaign trail, Mr. Speaker.
When we read the headlines in newspapers across the country we find "Minister on Collision Course with PM". Another headline reads "PM is Scaring People, Mayor Says". Another reads "PM Urged to Explain". Another one reads "Government Blamed for Inflation". Another one reads "Trudeau's Way of Fighting Inflation Worries Toronto Liberal Leaders". Another one reads "Trudeau Scheme Absolute". Another reads "Insanity". Another reads "Mr. Trudeau Is Wrong On Economy-It Is Government Out Of Joint". Another one reads "Destroy Trudeau-Carr". He is a labour leader. These are great comments coming from Canadians about our Prime Minister. Another reads "100,000 Cubans Cheer PM;. Castro's Welcome Top Level". Another reads "Could Trudeau Pull a Ghandi?" Another refers to Trudeau as Mr. Hitler.
If we are going to be faced with these sorts of things, I can see no better time to call an election in Canada. Another headline reads "Bankers Gloomy Over Canada's Long Term Prospects".

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-TRANSFER OF FOOD STOCKS FROM LOBLAWS TO ZIGGY'S-SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF JUSTIFICATION FOR PRICE INCREASE
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-TRANSFER OF FOOD STOCKS FROM LOBLAWS TO ZIGGY'S-SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF JUSTIFICATION FOR PRICE INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 7, 1975,1 brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) the fact that Loblaws Pickering Farms in Toronto had closed and reopened on October 18, after the announcement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of his anti-inflation policy, under the name of Ziggy's, which is also a Loblaws operation but with significantly higher prices.
The matter was referred to the Anti-Inflation Board by the minister, and last week that board made known its findings. The Anti-Inflation Board in its statement said, among other things, and I quote: "The decision of Loblaws was part of their ongoing marketing strategy".
It is no surprise that the board makes these kinds of decisions regarding prices. Board member Beryl Plumptre made it clear where she stood when she said:
The board will have to show restraint with companies and their profits. After all, we need profits to provide jobs and investment for more growth and more jobs.
Board chairman Jean-Luc Pepin also made it pretty clear where the board stands on prices, and he is quoted as saying the following:
Only by the end of the year, after we're able to study the big companies' profit reports will we be able to say that we've had an effect on prices here or touched something there. These guidelines on prices are much more difficult to put into use than the ones on wages.
That is what he said, again stating the obvious. Mr. Pepin accused the reporters of wanting instant coffee in terms of results on price controls. Obviously he was talking about instant coffee from Ziggy's, which now costs 20 per cent more.
In bringing down the Ziggy's decision Mr. John Hague, the director of the Anti-Inflation Board's prices and profits branch, said the decision was made to allow Loblaws to change its name to Ziggy's and raise its prices because the

increases were the result of normal business practices and decisions taken prior to the implementation of the program. No doubt it took Mr. Hague's group a very long time, since November 7 until last week, to come up with that excuse. I mean, here is an excuse that not only lets these Weston-owned stores off the hook and allows them to raise prices as much as they want, but they set a terrific precedent for other businesses. I will bet that executives across this country are still scrounging through their files looking for memos talking about price rises dated before October 14.
It looks as if any price increases in this country will be getting red carpet treatment from the government and its flunkies on the Anti-Inflation Board. I am confident enough in this country's corporations to be sure that, no matter how excessive and unreasonable their price increases are, they will be able to come up with a memo dated before October 14 to back them up.
I notice that these sorts of regulations do not apply to unions, however. Loblaws decides to change its name to Ziggy's before October 14 so they can raise their prices as much as they want. But unions which had their contracts expire before that date and which were negotiating with employers have no such luck.
Say the two parties to the negotiation have agreed to negotiate. They have agreed to come to an agreement satisfactory to both of them, regardless of how much that is. Surely, using the logic of Ziggy's, anyone whose contract expired before October 14 should be able to bargain without the interference of the Anti-Inflation Board. But it does not work that way. You can only pull that kind of a stunt if you own a multi-million dollar corporation.
The board is not even content just to roll back wages, its only real function. Instead it feels compelled to jump in on the side of employers in every collective dispute it sees. And Jean-Luc Pepin in not content just to be the government's pet crocodile, snapping at the wages of workers whenever he can; he now sometimes even feels compelled to mouth the Liberal party line as well. He apologized to the Conservative Party leader for some of his partisan remarks, but it is clear he has in no way changed his mind.
The government made it clear what this program is all about through the Anti-Inflation Board's announcement on Ziggy's. It might as well have erected billboards telling the corporations, "Help yourselves-no price interference here!"
In fact the only price freezes we have seen around here have been ones the supermarkets put on themselves. Those, the Globe and Mail discovered, included prices which were frozen higher than they should have been in the first place.
There is only one good thing which can be said about the Anti-Inflation Board's Ziggy's decision, and that is it is decisions like these which indicate that the board might be committing suicide. It is decisions like these which show the people of Canada what a hypocritical farce and fraud are being perpetrated on them.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-TRANSFER OF FOOD STOCKS FROM LOBLAWS TO ZIGGY'S-SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION OF JUSTIFICATION FOR PRICE INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Anti-Inflation Board has carried out an investigation of a report that a Loblaws Pickering Farms store located at
February 3, 1976

Yorkville Avenue and Yonge Street in downtown Toronto closed on October 18, 1975, and re-opened two weeks later as Ziggy's, a specialty chain owned by Loblaws, with higher prices.
The board's investigation disclosed no evidence that indicated the change in question was in any way an attempt on the part of Loblaws to circumvent the antiinflation guidelines. It was determined that Loblaws was in the process of rationalizing supermarket operations by closing down unprofitable stores. During the past four years, 110 supermarkets were closed. On October 18, 1975, the Loblaws store located at 852 Yonge Street, in Toronto, closed down and re-opened on October 30, 1975, as a Ziggy's operation, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Loblaws Ltd. The Ziggy's store in question operates as a specialty delicatessen store and carries, in addition to the regular Ziggy's product line, certain convenience products similar to Beckers, Mac's Milk, etc. Certain of these convenience products are common to both Ziggy's and Loblaws, and initially some prices were higher at Ziggy's. After public outcry, prices were immediately rolled back by Ziggy's. Therefore
Adjournment Debate
the decision to close the Loblaws store and to open as a Ziggy's outlet would not appear to contravene the guidelines.
The characteristics of Ziggy's are sufficiently different from that of a supermarket in that it offers specialty merchandise, uses special equipment, and renders a personal service that a special pricing policy would seem justified. However, the so-called convenience products, such as bread, milk, eggs, sugar, coffee, salt, etc., offered for the shopper's convenience only, and which do not fall under Ziggy's normal pricing policy, in the judgment of the board, should be priced in accordance with Loblaws' pricing methods. To this end the board has told Loblaws that the maximum price to be charged for these so-called convenience products at Ziggy's should not be priced higher than these same goods at Loblaws supermarkets. Loblaws have agreed to abide by this decision of the Anti-Inflation Board.
